With Kafri, Ceryl Tan and Nish Patel, she co-developed AoF (Assay of Feedback), a method that reconstructs how a signal changes over time from ordinary fixed-cell snapshots, without perturbing the pathway. Applied to Akt phosphorylation, it uncovered a negative feedback loop confined to a narrow window at the G1/S transition — a signature the group traces, cautiously, to mTORC1/S6K1-dependent inhibition of IRS1.

highlights.GIN2026: Co-develops AoF, a perturbation-free single-cell imaging method that reads a signal's rate of change from still images, and uses it to uncover a narrow G1/S-restricted Akt feedback loop plausibly traced to mTORC1/S6K1.

Ginzberg M.credit: Portrait: Kafri Lab, The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids)

Kafri R.role: Studies how mTORC1 sets and enforces a target size for cells
Kafri R.sub: Senior Scientist, Cell & Systems Biology, Hospital for Sick Children · Assistant Professor, Molecular Genetics, University of Toronto · Canada Research Chair (Tier 2), Quantitative Cell Biology · PhD, Weizmann Institute of Science
story: Ran Kafri trained at the Weizmann Institute of Science before building a lab at the Hospital for Sick Children and the University of Toronto around a deceptively simple question: what decides how big a cell gets, and how does it stay that size? His group has traced cell-size homeostasis to mTORC1 activity, and asks whether shifts in a person's mTORC1 'setpoint' over a lifetime could help explain cancer risk.

The AoF method his lab co-developed — reading a signal's dynamics out of fixed-cell snapshots rather than live imaging — extends that programme into feedback control itself, and its first application already lands on mTORC1: a narrow, cell-cycle-restricted window of Akt feedback the group attributes to mTORC1/S6K1 acting on IRS1.

highlights.GIN2026: Senior author on AoF, a snapshot-based method for inferring feedback dynamics, applied here to uncover a cell-cycle-restricted Akt feedback loop plausibly traced to mTORC1/S6K1.

Kafri R.credit: Portrait: Kafri Lab, The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids)

Lu L.role: Built a computational model treating mTORC1 as a rhythm set by meal timing, not a fixed level
Lu L.sub: PhD student, Department of Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, Rutgers University · Androulakis Lab
story: Lingjun Lu is a PhD student in Ioannis Androulakis' systems-biology group at Rutgers, working on computational models of how the liver's circadian clock is entrained by diet. In LU2026, she built a semi-mechanistic model in which mTORC1 and the GCN2-integrated stress response are driven by the rhythm of essential amino acid availability across the day, rather than by a single average nutrient level, and used it to predict how a disrupted feeding schedule delays the clock's recovery.

highlights.LU2026: Builds a computational model treating mTORC1 as a rhythm set by the timing and quality of amino acid intake, not a fixed level, and models how that rhythm's shape affects ribosome biogenesis.

Androulakis IP.role: Models how circadian rhythm and nutrient-sensing pathways like mTORC1 stay synchronized
Androulakis IP.sub: Professor, Biomedical Engineering & Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, Rutgers University · adjunct, Department of Surgery, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School · PhD, Chemical Engineering, Purdue University (1993)
story: Ioannis Androulakis runs a systems-biology and -pharmacology group at Rutgers focused on the interactions between circadian rhythms, inflammation and metabolism. In LU2026, his group built a mathematical model of the liver's peripheral clock in which mTORC1 and GCN2-ISR signalling jointly determine how well the clock stays synchronized to feeding rhythms under nutrient stress — a computational companion to the experimental case, elsewhere in this Atlas, that mTORC1's pattern over time, not just its average level, is what matters.

highlights.LU2026: Senior author on a model in which liver mTORC1 and GCN2-ISR signalling jointly set circadian entrainability, predicting individualized recovery trajectories after a disrupted feeding schedule.

Androulakis IP.credit: Portrait: Rutgers University, Dept. of Biomedical Engineering

Wang R.role: Built FPTT, fluorescent 'ticker tapes' that record several signalling pathways in living cells over days, and used its mTOR version to follow mTOR activity oscillating through the cell cycle
Wang R.sub: PhD (2026), School of Life Sciences, Westlake University · Piatkevich Lab (graduate student 2021–2026) · College of Life Sciences, Zhejiang University
story: Ruizhao Wang completed a PhD in 2026 in Kiryl Piatkevich's lab at Westlake University, in a joint program with Zhejiang University, building fluorescent-protein tools that record how signalling pathways change over time inside living cells. As first author of WANG2026C, Wang designed the fluorescent protein ticker tape (FPTT): multispectral fluorescent proteins fused to self-assembling protein fibres, so that a cell's promoter activity is written onto a growing fibre as a colour-coded timeline. The system logged cFos activity in hippocampal neurons at 3-hour resolution over 8 days, and the team built versions for several pathways, including one for mTOR that showed mTOR activity oscillating with the cell cycle, a pattern also reported in JOS2024 with a different method.
Ruizhao Wang is a different person from Ruoning Wang (St. Jude, now Nationwide Children's Hospital), who shares the same short citation form, Wang R.

highlights.WANG2026C: First author: built the FPTT recording platform, including an mTOR recorder that tracked mTOR activity oscillating through the cell cycle.

Jiang J.role: Co-developed FPTT, fluorescent 'ticker tapes' that record several signalling pathways in living cells over days, including an mTOR recorder that tracked mTOR activity oscillating through the cell cycle
Jiang J.sub: School of Life Sciences, Westlake University · School of Life Sciences, Fudan University
story: Jian Jiang is a co-author of WANG2026C, with affiliations at the School of Life Sciences of Westlake University and of Fudan University, consistent with the joint PhD program the two universities run. The study, led from Kiryl Piatkevich's lab, built FPTT (fluorescent protein ticker tape), a way to record the history of a signalling pathway over days in single living cells. The team made FPTT versions for several major pathways, including mTOR, and used the mTOR version to show that mTOR activity rises and falls with the cell cycle, a pattern also reported in JOS2024 with a different method.

highlights.WANG2026C: Co-developed the FPTT multiplexed biosensor system, whose mTOR version showed mTOR activity oscillating with the cell cycle.

Schreiber SL.role: Co-discovered mTOR in 1994 (his group called it FRAP) as the mammalian target of the FKBP12–rapamycin complex, and helped found chemical biology as a field
Schreiber SL.sub: Chief Scientific Officer, Arena BioWorks (since 2025) · Morris Loeb Professor of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University (1988–present, now Emeritus) · co-founder of the Broad Institute · HHMI Investigator (Emeritus) · assistant professor, Yale University (1980) · PhD, Harvard University (Robert B. Woodward, then Yoshito Kishi) · BA in chemistry, University of Virginia
story: In 1994, Schreiber's lab purified the mammalian protein that binds the immunosuppressant complex FKBP12–rapamycin — naming it FRAP, later renamed mTOR — and showed it was the human homolog of yeast TOR1/TOR2, the genes originally implicated in rapamycin's growth-arresting effects. Two years later, his group solved the crystal structure of FKBP12–rapamycin bound to mTOR's FRB domain, revealing the atomic mechanism: a single rapamycin molecule sits in the interface and plugs into two separate hydrophobic pockets, one on FKBP12 and one on FRB, physically gluing the two proteins together. That structure became a founding example of a 'molecular glue' — a small molecule that works not by blocking a single active site but by forcing two proteins into an unnatural complex, a concept that now underlies an entire class of drugs (including PROTACs).

Schreiber trained in organic synthesis at Harvard, first under Robert B. Woodward and then Yoshito Kishi after Woodward's death, before starting his own lab at Yale in 1980 and returning to Harvard in 1988. Through the 1990s he helped found the field of chemical biology, developing diversity-oriented synthesis — methods for building large, structurally diverse small-molecule collections — as a way to probe biology the way genetics probes it with mutations. In 1997 he became founding director of Harvard's Institute of Chemistry and Cell Biology, whose screening infrastructure and chemical-genetics philosophy fed directly into the 2004 founding of the Broad Institute, where he built and led its Chemical Biology Program.

Schreiber is a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator (now Emeritus) and a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the National Academy of Medicine, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences; he has received the Wolf Prize in Chemistry, among other honors. In 2024 he co-founded Arena BioWorks, a privately funded, non-profit biomedical research institute in Cambridge, MA, where he now serves as Chief Scientific Officer.

highlights.BRO1994: Purifies FRAP (now called mTOR) as the mammalian protein bound by the FKBP12–rapamycin complex, identifying the direct molecular target of rapamycin.
highlights.CHO1996: Solves the crystal structure of FKBP12–rapamycin bound to mTOR's FRB domain, showing rapamycin acts as a molecular glue that plugs into two protein pockets at once.

Sonenberg N.role: Discovered the mRNA cap-binding protein eIF4E and the 4E-BP proteins that restrain it, and showed how mTOR releases this brake to control protein synthesis
Sonenberg N.sub: James McGill Professor of Biochemistry and Gilman Cheney Chair, McGill University; Director, Rosalind and Morris Goodman Cancer Research Centre · joined McGill University (1979) · postdoc, Roche Institute of Molecular Biology (Aaron Shatkin lab) · PhD, Weizmann Institute of Science (1976) · BSc & MSc in microbiology and immunology, Tel Aviv University
story: In 1999, Sonenberg's group worked out how the translational repressor 4E-BP1 is actually switched off: rather than being phosphorylated all at once, it is modified through an ordered, priming two-step mechanism, in which phosphorylation at certain sites must occur before others can follow, and only the fully phosphorylated protein releases its grip on the cap-binding protein eIF4E. Since eIF4E is the factor that recognizes the 5' cap of mRNA and recruits it into the ribosome, this phosphorylation cascade — which sits downstream of mTORC1 — acts as a molecular switch that turns on cap-dependent protein synthesis when nutrients and growth signals are abundant. In 2013, his lab extended this logic to metabolism, showing that mTORC1, acting specifically through 4E-BP-dependent control of translation, regulates the biogenesis and activity of mitochondria.

Sonenberg did his PhD at the Weizmann Institute of Science and then a postdoctoral fellowship with Aaron Shatkin at the Roche Institute of Molecular Biology, where the two identified eIF4E, the protein that binds the 5' cap of messenger RNA — the discovery that set the direction for his entire career studying translational control. He joined McGill University's Department of Biochemistry in 1979 and has remained there since.

Sonenberg is a Fellow of the Royal Society, an Officer of the Order of Canada, and a Foreign Associate of the US National Academy of Sciences; his honors include the Gairdner Foundation International Award and the Wolf Prize in Medicine. He currently holds the Gilman Cheney Chair in Biochemistry at McGill and directs the Rosalind and Morris Goodman Cancer Research Centre.

highlights.GIN1999: Shows that 4E-BP1 phosphorylation follows an ordered, priming two-step mechanism that determines when 4E-BP1 releases eIF4E to permit cap-dependent translation.
highlights.MOR2013: Shows that mTORC1 controls mitochondrial biogenesis and activity specifically through 4E-BP-dependent regulation of translation.

Alessi DR.lab_name: Principal investigator page, MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, University of Dundee
Alessi DR.role: Discovered PDK1, the master kinase that switches on Akt and related AGC kinases, and showed that mTORC2 activates the kinase SGK1
Alessi DR.sub: Director, MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit, University of Dundee (since 2012) · Professor of Signal Transduction, University of Dundee (since 2003) · postdoc, University of Dundee (Philip Cohen lab, 1991–1997) · PhD, University of Birmingham (1991) · BSc, University of Birmingham (1988)
story: In 1997, working in Philip Cohen's Dundee lab, Alessi purified and characterised PDK1 — the kinase that phosphorylates Akt/PKB on its activation-loop threonine (Thr308) in response to PI3K-generated lipids, switching the enzyme on. PDK1 turned out to be a hub: it also activates p70 S6 kinase and other AGC-family kinases, placing it structurally upstream of, and mechanistically intertwined with, mTOR signalling. He later extended this into the mTORC2 side of the pathway: with Jose M. Garcia-Martinez, his group showed that mTORC2 phosphorylates not only Akt's hydrophobic motif but also that of SGK1 (2008), meaning mTORC2 sits at the top of two parallel growth-factor-response kinases, not one. The following year the same collaboration produced Ku-0063794, one of the first genuinely selective ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors — blocking both mTORC1 and mTORC2 — which became widely used to dissect which of mTOR's effects depend on each complex.

Alessi trained in biochemistry at the University of Birmingham, then moved to Dundee for postdoctoral work with Philip Cohen — a lab already central to phosphorylation research — where he stayed on as an independent program leader from 1997. He became Professor of Signal Transduction at Dundee in 2003 and was appointed Director of what is now the MRC Protein Phosphorylation and Ubiquitylation Unit in 2012.

His current work centres on LRRK2 and the phosphorylation pathways implicated in inherited Parkinson's disease, alongside the Division of Signal Transduction Therapy, a long-running collaboration between the Dundee unit and major pharmaceutical companies. He is a Fellow of the Royal Society (2008) and the Academy of Medical Sciences, and was appointed OBE in 2023.

highlights.GAR2008: Shows that mTORC2 controls the hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation and activation of SGK1, extending mTORC2's reach beyond Akt to a second growth-factor-responsive kinase.
highlights.GAR2009: Characterises Ku-0063794 as a specific ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor that blocks both mTORC1 and mTORC2, becoming a standard tool for separating the two complexes' effects.

Alessi DR.credit: Portrait: MRC PPU, University of Dundee

Pavletich NP.lab_name: Pavletich Lab, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Pavletich NP.role: Solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, revealing the FRB domain as a gatekeeper of its active site, and later showed how RHEB switches mTORC1 on and PRAS40 blocks it
Pavletich NP.sub: Stephen and Barbara Friedman Chair, Sloan Kettering Institute · Chair, Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center · faculty, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (since 1993) · HHMI Investigator (1997–2022) · postdoc, MIT (Carl Pabo lab) · PhD, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (1991) · BS in Chemistry, Caltech (1988)
story: In 2013, Pavletich's lab solved the first crystal structure of the mTOR kinase domain itself — a feat that had eluded structural biologists for years because mTOR is a huge, flexible, membrane-associated enzyme. The structure showed why mTOR's active site is so hard for drugs and substrates to reach: it sits in a deep recess, and the FRB domain acts as a lid or 'gatekeeper' controlling access, explaining at the atomic level exactly how the FKBP12–rapamycin complex jams the site shut, and why activating cancer mutations cluster around it. In 2017, his group followed up with structures of the full mTORC1 complex bound to its regulators, showing mechanistically how the small GTPase RHEB docks onto mTOR and allosterically realigns its catalytic residues to turn the kinase on, while the inhibitory subunit PRAS40 works by occluding the substrate-binding surface.

The mTOR work came after two decades in which Pavletich's lab built a track record of solving landmark, previously 'unsolvable' cancer-related protein structures by X-ray crystallography: the p53 tumour-suppressor core domain bound to DNA (1994); the MDM2–p53 transactivation-domain complex, which defined the druggable pocket later exploited by MDM2-inhibitor cancer drugs such as the Nutlins (1996); the p27Kip1–cyclin A–Cdk2 complex, showing how p27 both rearranges and physically plugs the kinase's ATP cleft to halt the cell cycle (1996); and the VHL–ElonginC–ElonginB complex, revealing the tumorigenic hot-spot on the von Hippel–Lindau protein (1999).

Pavletich trained in chemistry at Caltech, earned his PhD at Johns Hopkins, and did postdoctoral work with Carl Pabo at MIT before joining Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center's faculty in 1993, becoming an HHMI Investigator in 1997 and Chair of the Structural Biology Program in 2003. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2012. His lab's current focus has extended from mTOR to the structural biology of DNA-damage-response machinery, including the ATR and ATM checkpoint kinases and the Fanconi anemia pathway.

highlights.YAN2013: Solves the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase domain, showing how its FRB domain gates a deeply buried active site and how FKBP12-rapamycin blocks it.
highlights.YAN2017: Determines structures of mTORC1 bound to its regulators, showing how RHEB allosterically activates the kinase while PRAS40 holds it inhibited.

Pavletich NP.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Harper JW.role: Co-discovered the F-box motif that links substrates to SCF ubiquitin ligases, and co-leads with Steven Gygi the BioPlex protein-interaction map, which contributed to the discoveries of the CASTOR and SAMTOR nutrient sensors
Harper JW.sub: Bert and Natalie Vallee Professor of Molecular Pathology and Chair, Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (since 2003; chair since 2014) · faculty, Department of Biochemistry, Baylor College of Medicine (1988–2003) · postdoc, Harvard Medical School (Bert Vallee lab) · PhD in Chemistry, Georgia Institute of Technology (1984)
story: Harper's contribution to two of the Atlas's mTORC1 nutrient-sensing papers came from the interactome side of the problem, not the sensing biochemistry itself. His group, working with Steven Gygi's mass-spectrometry lab, built BioPlex — a systematic map of human protein–protein interactions made by tagging thousands of individual proteins, pulling each one out of cells, and identifying everything that co-purifies with it. When the Sabatini lab wanted to know what else physically touches the GATOR2 amino-acid-sensing complex, they searched BioPlex rather than starting from scratch: two 'previously uncharacterized' genes turned up as GATOR2 interactors and became CASTOR1 and CASTOR2 (2016). A year later, mining an expanded version of BioPlex for GATOR1/KICSTOR partners flagged another orphan gene, later renamed SAMTOR (2017). In both cases, the Harper–Gygi interaction map is what handed the Sabatini lab the candidate protein before any of the nutrient-binding biochemistry began.

Harper trained as a chemist before moving into protein biochemistry as a postdoc with Bert Vallee at Harvard Medical School, then spent 15 years on the Baylor College of Medicine faculty. It was at Baylor, in 1996, that his group — working with Stephen Elledge's lab — identified the F-box, a short protein motif that lets 'substrate receptor' proteins dock onto the SCF (Skp1–Cullin1–F-box) ubiquitin ligase complex, explaining how the cell's protein-degradation machinery achieves substrate specificity across the cell cycle.

Harper returned to Harvard Medical School in 2003 (department chair since 2014). His lab has since built some of the field's key large-scale interactome and quantitative-proteomics resources (BioPlex among them) and used them to dissect the PARKIN ubiquitin ligase's role in clearing damaged mitochondria (mitophagy), work directly relevant to Parkinson's disease. He was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (2018) and the National Academy of Sciences (2023).

highlights.CHA2016: Co-built BioPlex, the immunoprecipitation-mass-spectrometry interactome dataset that first flagged the uncharacterized protein GATSL3 (CASTOR1) as a GATOR2 binding partner.
highlights.GU2017: Co-built the expanded BioPlex interactome that, when mined for GATOR1/KICSTOR partners, flagged the uncharacterized protein C7orf60 — later renamed SAMTOR.

Harper JW.credit: Portrait: Harper Lab, Harvard Medical School

Gygi SP.role: Mass-spectrometry pioneer whose Harvard lab builds large-scale proteomics methods, including the BioPlex human protein-interaction map, and contributed proteomics to the discoveries of the CASTOR and SAMTOR nutrient sensors
Gygi SP.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School; faculty director, Taplin Biological Mass Spectrometry Facility and the Thermo Fisher Center for Multiplexed Proteomics · own lab, Harvard Medical School (since 2000) · postdoc, University of Washington (Ruedi Aebersold lab, from 1996) · PhD in Pharmacology and Toxicology (mass spectrometry), University of Utah
story: Gygi's lab supplied the identification step behind the Atlas's two BioPlex-derived nutrient-sensor papers: after Wade Harper's group immunoprecipitated a tagged 'bait' protein out of cells, it was Gygi's mass spectrometers that identified every protein sticking to it, repeated across thousands of different baits to build BioPlex. That pipeline is what put CASTOR1 (then an obscure gene, GATSL3) on a list of GATOR2-interacting proteins in 2016, and what flagged SAMTOR (then C7orf60) as a GATOR1/KICSTOR partner in 2017 — both times before anyone knew these proteins bound a nutrient at all. Screens at that scale exist mainly because Gygi's group has spent two decades making quantitative mass spectrometry faster, more sensitive, and multiplexable.

Gygi earned his PhD at the University of Utah on small-molecule mass spectrometry, then did a postdoctoral fellowship (from 1996) with Ruedi Aebersold at the University of Washington, one of the labs that founded modern quantitative proteomics. Since starting his own lab at Harvard Medical School in 2000, Gygi has been a driving force behind Tandem Mass Tag (TMT) multiplexing, which lets many samples be compared in a single mass-spec run, and more recently TMTpro, which pushed that to 16 samples at once.

He now directs two HMS core mass-spectrometry facilities — the Taplin Biological Mass Spectrometry Facility and the Thermo Fisher Center for Multiplexed Proteomics — that generate proteomic and interactome data used throughout cancer biology, neuroscience, and cell biology well beyond his own lab's projects.

highlights.CHA2016: Performed the mass-spectrometry identification behind BioPlex that first showed the uncharacterized protein GATSL3 (CASTOR1) co-purifying with the GATOR2 complex.
highlights.GU2017: Performed the mass-spectrometry profiling behind the expanded BioPlex network that identified the uncharacterized protein C7orf60 (SAMTOR) as a GATOR1/KICSTOR interactor.

Shokat KM.role: Co-invented the ATP-competitive 'TORKinib' mTOR inhibitors that block both mTORC1 and mTORC2, and later RapaLink-1, a third-generation inhibitor that overcomes mTOR resistance mutations
Shokat KM.sub: Professor of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, UC San Francisco, joint appointment in Chemistry at UC Berkeley, and HHMI Investigator (since 2005) · faculty, Princeton University · postdoc, Stanford University (Christopher Goodnow lab) · PhD, UC Berkeley (Peter G. Schultz lab) · BA, Reed College
story: Rapamycin is an allosteric mTORC1 inhibitor: it only partly suppresses the complex and doesn't touch mTORC2 at all, so cap-dependent translation driven by 4E-BP1 phosphorylation often survives treatment. In 2009, Shokat's group solved this by building small molecules that instead plug directly into mTOR's ATP-binding pocket — the kinase's active site, shared by both mTORC1 and mTORC2. These "TORKinibs" (PP242, PP30) shut down both complexes at once and, unlike rapamycin, fully collapse cap-dependent translation. Christopher Thoreen and David Sabatini's lab reached the same conclusion independently and simultaneously with their inhibitor Torin1 — together the two papers defined an entire new class of mTOR drugs built on chemistry rather than the natural product rapamycin.

Shokat trained as a chemist, earning his PhD at Berkeley with Peter Schultz working on catalytic antibodies, then moved into biology as a postdoc with immunologist Christopher Goodnow at Stanford, studying tyrosine kinases in B-cell tolerance. His own Princeton lab pioneered 'bump-and-hole' engineering — mutating a kinase's ATP pocket and pairing it with a matched, cell-permeable ATP analog so that one specific kinase, out of hundreds in the genome, can be selectively inhibited or traced to its direct substrates.

That chemical toolkit later turned toward oncogenic signaling: in 2013 his lab published the first covalent inhibitors of KRAS G12C, exploiting a cysteine created by the mutation to lock the oncoprotein in its inactive, GDP-bound state — turning a target long dismissed as 'undruggable' into the basis for an entire clinical drug class (sotorasib, adagrasib, and successors). He is a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the National Academy of Medicine, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and continues to run an active chemical biology lab at UCSF alongside his HHMI investigatorship.

highlights.FEL2009: Introduces ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors (PP242, PP30) that hit both mTORC1 and mTORC2, shutting down the cap-dependent translation that rapamycin leaves intact.
highlights.ROD2016: Introduces RapaLink-1, a bivalent third-generation mTOR inhibitor that overcomes resistance mutations that defeat both rapalogs and first-generation TORKinibs.

Pandolfi PP.lab_name: Professional profile, William N. Pennington Cancer Institute, Renown Health / DRI
Pandolfi PP.role: Showed that ERK directly phosphorylates and inactivates TSC2, wiring Ras/MAPK signalling into mTORC1 control, and that blocking mTORC1 in patients' tumours triggers a feedback rise in MAPK signalling
Pandolfi PP.sub: Scientific Director, William N. Pennington Cancer Institute, Renown Health, with Desert Research Institute, Reno NV (since 2020) · Director of Cancer Genetics, then Cancer Research Institute, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School (2007–2019) · faculty, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center & Weill Cornell Medical College (1994–2007) · postgraduate research, Royal Postgraduate Medical School, London (Arthur Zelent lab) · MD (1989) and PhD (1995), University of Perugia
story: Akt is the textbook route that inactivates the TSC1–TSC2 brake on mTORC1, but it isn't the only one. In 2005, Pandolfi's group showed that ERK — the kinase at the business end of the Ras/MAPK growth pathway — directly phosphorylates TSC2 at sites distinct from Akt's, and that this is enough to functionally inactivate the TSC complex on its own. That gives mTORC1 a second, independent input arm alongside PI3K/Akt and AMPK. His group extended this logic clinically in 2008, showing that inhibiting mTORC1 with rapalogs in cancer cells paradoxically activates MAPK/ERK signaling through a PI3K-dependent feedback loop — one of the key mechanistic reasons single-node mTOR inhibitors often disappoint as cancer monotherapies.

Pandolfi's research career began as an MD/PhD student in Perugia studying acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), then continued as a postdoctoral researcher in London, where his transgenic-mouse work helped explain why PML-RARA-driven APL responds to retinoic acid while PLZF-RARA-driven APL does not. At Memorial Sloan-Kettering and Weill Cornell (1994–2007) his lab built the Pten knockout mouse, establishing PTEN as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor. At Beth Israel Deaconess / Harvard Medical School (2007–2019) his group proposed the competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) hypothesis — that a pseudogene's mRNA can act as a molecular 'sponge' for microRNAs and thereby regulate a protein-coding gene like PTEN.

Since 2020 Pandolfi has directed cancer research at the William N. Pennington Cancer Institute, Renown Health, jointly with the Desert Research Institute, in Reno, Nevada. He continues to publish on APL, PTEN/PI3K–mTOR signaling, and cancer genetics.

highlights.MA2005: Shows that ERK directly phosphorylates and inactivates TSC2, giving Ras/MAPK signaling a route into mTORC1 activation that runs independently of PI3K/Akt.
highlights.CAR2008: Shows that inhibiting mTORC1 in human cancer cells activates MAPK pathway signaling through a PI3K-dependent feedback loop.

Kennedy BK.lab_name: Faculty profile, National University of Singapore
Kennedy BK.role: Showed with Matt Kaeberlein that reducing TOR or Sch9 signalling extends yeast lifespan in the same way as dietary restriction, and has since championed mTOR as a target for slowing human ageing
Kennedy BK.sub: Distinguished Professor of Biochemistry & Physiology, National University of Singapore (since 2017) · President & CEO, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (2010–2016) · Assistant/Associate Professor, University of Washington (with Matt Kaeberlein) · postdoc, Massachusetts General Hospital Cancer Center · PhD, MIT (Leonard Guarente lab)
story: In 2005, Kennedy and Matt Kaeberlein, working together at the University of Washington, systematically deleted 564 individual genes in yeast and measured how long each mutant strain lived. The strongest lifespan-extending hits, by a wide margin, were genes in the TOR (Target Of Rapamycin) and Sch9 pathway — the first genome-scale evidence, rather than a single-gene hunch, that dialing down nutrient-sensing signaling through TOR is one of the most powerful levers for extending lifespan, in an organism as simple as budding yeast.

Kennedy trained with Leonard Guarente at MIT, whose lab had linked sirtuins to yeast aging, then moved into aging research proper as a UW faculty member working alongside Kaeberlein. In 2010 he took over as President and CEO of the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, where he spent six years building it into one of the field's leading independent aging-research institutes.

Since 2017 Kennedy has been Distinguished Professor of Biochemistry and Physiology at the National University of Singapore, where he directs the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Programme — work focused on translating basic geroscience, including TOR biology, into biomarkers and interventions that could delay human aging rather than just treat individual age-related diseases.

highlights.KAE2005: A systematic screen of 564 yeast gene deletions identifies TOR and Sch9 pathway genes as the single strongest lifespan-extending hits, establishing nutrient-sensing signaling as a central, targetable axis of aging.
highlights.KEN2016: A review argues mTOR acts as the coordinating hub of whole-body metabolism and lays out why mTORC2 inhibition underlies rapamycin's metabolic side effects — the main obstacle to repurposing it as an anti-aging drug.

Partridge L.lab_name: Emerita profile, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing
Partridge L.role: Showed that rapamycin extends fruit-fly lifespan through TORC1, via autophagy and reduced protein synthesis, and that it adds benefit even on top of dietary restriction
Partridge L.sub: Emerita Professor, UCL and Emeritus Scientific Member, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing · founding director, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Cologne (2008–2023) · Weldon Professor of Biometry, University College London (from 1994; director, UCL Institute of Healthy Ageing, 2007–2019) · Professor of Evolutionary Biology, University of Edinburgh · postdoc, University of York · DPhil, University of Oxford
story: Partridge's 2010 paper with Ivana Bjedov showed that simply adding rapamycin to fruit fly food extended their lifespan, and traced the mechanism: rapamycin's mTOR inhibition boosted autophagy (the cell's internal recycling system) and reduced general protein synthesis — the same two downstream effects long suspected to explain why eating less extends lifespan. Critically, rapamycin still worked even in flies already eating a lifespan-optimized diet, showing that drugging TOR directly can extend life beyond what diet alone achieves.

That result connected to the broader synthesis she co-authored with Luigi Fontana and Valter Longo in Science that same year, which laid out the evidence that dietary restriction and reduced signaling through nutrient-sensing pathways — insulin/IGF-1 and TOR — extend healthy lifespan by conserved mechanisms running from yeast through worms and flies to primates and humans.

Partridge built her career using Drosophila as a genetically tractable model for the evolutionary biology and mechanisms of aging, moving from Edinburgh to UCL's Weldon Chair of Biometry in 1994 and later founding the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing in Cologne in 2008, which she directed until her retirement in 2023. She was elected FRS in 1996, made DBE in 2009, and delivered the Royal Society's Croonian Medal Lecture the same year, alongside the Darwin–Wallace Medal from the Linnean Society.

highlights.FON2010: A landmark synthesis showing that dietary restriction and dampened nutrient-sensing signaling — mTOR and growth hormone/IGF-1 — extend healthy lifespan by conserved mechanisms from yeast to primates and humans.
highlights.BJE2010: Feeding rapamycin to fruit flies extends lifespan via increased autophagy and reduced translation, and still works even in flies already on a lifespan-maximizing diet.

Kopchick JJ.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Ohio University (formerly Edison Biotechnology Institute)
Kopchick JJ.role: Discovered the growth hormone receptor antagonist that became the acromegaly drug pegvisomant (Somavert), and studies how blocking growth hormone signalling extends lifespan in mice
Kopchick JJ.sub: Distinguished Professor & Goll-Ohio Eminent Scholar, Ohio University (since 2012) · Edison Biotechnology Institute, Ohio University (1987–present) · senior scientist, Merck Institute of Therapeutic Research (1982–1986) · postdoctoral fellow, Roche Institute of Molecular Biology (1980–1982) · PhD, University of Texas Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences at MD Anderson (1980)
story: Decades after his accidental 1987 discovery that a mutated growth hormone (GH) molecule could block rather than activate the GH receptor — work that became the FDA-approved drug pegvisomant — Kopchick's lab is now using the same logic to ask how far blocking GH action can extend life. In List et al. 2026 (LIST2026), his team engineered mice that transgenically express a GH receptor antagonist built on the same G119K mutant chemistry behind pegvisomant, and found it significantly extended both median and maximal lifespan in both sexes. A companion study, Duran-Ortiz et al. 2026 (DUR2026), showed that deleting the GH receptor gene starting only at 12 months of age (adult-onset) still extended healthy lifespan in both sexes.

Kopchick's original discovery happened almost by accident: while trying to engineer a bigger mouse, he instead produced a dwarf mouse. That molecule became Somavert (pegvisomant), still used worldwide to treat acromegaly, generating roughly $100+ million in licensing royalties for Ohio University. He trained at MD Anderson and the Roche Institute before six years at Merck, joining Ohio University in 1987.

He has since built one of the world's most extensive collections of GH-signaling mouse models, holds 17 patents, has published 400+ papers, is a National Academy of Inventors Fellow, and received the Endocrine Society's 2019 Laureate Award for Outstanding Innovation.

highlights.LIST2026: Kopchick's own antagonist chemistry — the molecular basis of pegvisomant — is shown for the first time to extend lifespan in mice when expressed transgenically.
highlights.DUR2026: As senior investigator, shows that even adult-onset disruption of GH receptor signaling extends healthy lifespan.

Berryman DE.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine
Berryman DE.role: Showed that growth hormone reshapes fat tissue in a depot-specific way that links body composition to metabolic aging
Berryman DE.sub: Professor of Biomedical Sciences & Associate Dean for Research and Innovation, Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine · Registered & Licensed Dietitian (2001) · PhD Nutritional Sciences, Cornell University (1994) · BS Biology, University of Virginia (1988)
story: In LIST2026, two-year-old mice expressing a GH receptor antagonist lived longer and were less frail — but also had increased adiposity, reflecting Berryman's long-running argument that fat tissue quality/distribution, not just quantity, drives metabolic outcomes under altered GH signaling. In DUR2026, adult-onset GH receptor deletion improved insulin sensitivity in males, and single-cell liver sequencing revealed sex-dimorphic remodeling.

Trained as a nutritional scientist at Cornell after a biology degree at UVA, she later earned dietetic credentials — unusual among molecular biologists. She built her program on how GH excess/deficiency reshapes adipose tissue.
She now serves as Associate Dean for Research and Innovation and has held interim leadership of the renamed Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging.

highlights.LIST2026: Contributes body-composition/frailty phenotyping showing lifespan-extending GH receptor antagonism paradoxically increases adiposity even while improving frailty markers.
highlights.DUR2026: Co-authors single-cell liver transcriptomics showing sex-specific metabolic remodeling after adult-onset GH receptor deletion.

List EO.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine
List EO.role: Leads the mouse studies defining how disrupting growth hormone receptor signaling extends mammalian lifespan
List EO.sub: Research Associate Professor of Biomedical Sciences, Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine · Associate Investigator, Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging · PhD, Ohio University
story: List is lead author of LIST2026, which showed GH-receptor-antagonist mice lived significantly longer, and co-author of DUR2026, showing adult-onset GH receptor deletion still extends healthy lifespan.
With a PhD from Ohio University, List has spent his career inside the GH/longevity mouse-model pipeline alongside Kopchick and Berryman, co-authoring dozens of core GHRKO papers.
He now runs much of the day-to-day mouse-aging experimental program at the renamed Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging.

highlights.LIST2026: As lead author, demonstrates transgenic GH receptor antagonist significantly extends median and maximal mouse lifespan.
highlights.DUR2026: Co-authors the finding that adult-onset GH receptor ablation extends healthy lifespan and improves insulin sensitivity.

Efeyan A.lab_name: Metabolism and Cell Signalling Group, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid
Efeyan A.role: Showed that mTORC1's amino-acid sensor, the Rag GTPases, is a life-or-death switch for newborn mice surviving the fast before their first feeding
Efeyan A.sub: Group Leader, CNIO (since 2016) · postdoc, Whitehead Institute, MIT (David M. Sabatini lab, 2008–2015) · PhD, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, CNIO (Manuel Serrano lab, 2003–2008)
story: As a postdoc with Sabatini, Efeyan helped show (ZON2011) that amino-acid sensing begins inside the lysosome: amino acids accumulating in the lumen are read by the v-ATPase, which relays an 'inside-out' signal to Ragulator-Rag to activate mTORC1. In 2012 he led his own study using knock-in mice with permanently active RagA — these mice die within a day of birth, unable to switch mTORC1 off during the neonatal fast, failing to induce autophagy or mobilize amino acids for gluconeogenesis.
Efeyan trained as a mouse geneticist in Manuel Serrano's lab (p53/tumor suppression) before 7 years with Sabatini.
In 2016 he returned to Madrid to start his own CNIO group studying nutrient sensing, cancer, and aging; named EMBO Young Investigator.

highlights.EFE2012: Knock-in mice with constitutively active RagA cannot switch off mTORC1 during the neonatal fast and die within a day of birth.
highlights.ZON2011: Amino-acid sensing begins inside the lysosome, relayed 'inside-out' via the v-ATPase to Ragulator-Rag.

Bodine SC.lab_name: Aging & Metabolism Research Program, Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation (OMRF)
Bodine SC.role: Showed that turning on the Akt-mTOR pathway is enough, by itself, to make skeletal muscle grow and to stop it from wasting away
Bodine SC.sub: Professor, OMRF (since 2023) · President, American Physiological Society (2026) · Professor, University of Iowa Carver College of Medicine (2017–2023) · Professor, UC Davis (2003–2017) · Lab Director, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (1996–2003) · PhD, UCLA (V. Reggie Edgerton lab, 1985)
story: In back-to-back 2001 Nature Cell Biology papers, Bodine's Regeneron group (BOD2001) and a companion Rommel et al. study (ROM2001, on which she was key author) established that activating Akt/mTOR is sufficient by itself to trigger muscle hypertrophy and prevent atrophy in vivo — rapamycin blocked hypertrophy in every model tested.

Bodine trained under V. Reggie Edgerton at UCLA (including Soviet Bion space-biology missions), directed muscle/nerve regeneration research at Regeneron, then built labs at UC Davis and University of Iowa extending the findings into disuse atrophy, sarcopenia, and atrogin-1/MuRF1 E3 ligases.
Since 2023 at OMRF; began a term as American Physiological Society president in 2026.

highlights.BOD2001: Activating Akt/mTOR alone triggers skeletal-muscle hypertrophy and blocks disuse atrophy; rapamycin blocks hypertrophy in every model.
highlights.ROM2001: IGF-1 drives myotube hypertrophy specifically through PI3K/Akt/mTOR and PI3K/Akt/GSK3.

Long X.lab_name: Avruch Lab, Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard Medical School
Long X.role: Discovered that Rheb binds directly to the mTOR kinase domain and switches it on
Long X.sub: Research staff, MGH/Harvard (Joseph Avruch lab, 2002–2009) · pre-2002 training and post-2009 career not publicly documented
story: By 2005 (LON2005), Long showed Rheb binds straight onto the mTOR kinase domain and that binding stimulates catalytic activity — a physical, mechanistic link between GTPase and kinase.

Long's traceable record sits entirely inside the Avruch lab, 2002–2009, ending with a 2009 review co-authorship. No public record before/after this window turned up — common for researchers from this era who moved into industry without a web footprint.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author on the founding Raptor paper (Avruch/Yonezawa collaboration).
highlights.LON2005: Rheb binds directly to the mTOR kinase domain and stimulates its activity.

Hara K.lab_name: Department of Diabetes & Endocrinology, Kita Harima Medical Center
Hara K.role: Showed in 1998 that amino acids are needed for mTOR to activate S6K1 and 4E-BP1, and as first author co-discovered raptor in 2002
Hara K.sub: Physician, Kita Harima Medical Center, Hyogo, Japan (most recent traceable publication, 2021) · Faculty, Kobe University Graduate School of Medicine · Researcher, Kobe University Biosignal Research Center (Kazuyoshi Yonezawa lab) · Postdoc, MGH/Harvard (Joseph Avruch lab)
story: In 1998 (HAR1998), Hara showed pulling amino acids from growth medium silences p70 S6K and 4E-BP1 even with insulin present — one of the first papers linking amino acids to mTOR. In 2002 he co-discovered Raptor (HARA2002), tying that finding to the scaffold protein executing it.

Returned to Japan/Kobe University, co-authoring further mTOR papers through the mid-2000s (incl. with Shinya Yamanaka's group, 2004). Later moved into clinical academic medicine (Internal & Geriatric Medicine, then Diabetes & Endocrinology).
Most recent traceable publication (2021, leucine/cardioprotection) lists him at Kita Harima Medical Center, a regional hospital — suggesting his career settled into clinical practice.

highlights.HARA2002: Lead investigator on the founding Raptor paper.
highlights.HAR1998: Amino acid sufficiency and mTOR regulate p70 S6K and 4E-BP1 through a shared mechanism.

Oshiro N.lab_name: Xavier Lab, MGH Center for Computational & Integrative Biology / Broad Institute
Oshiro N.role: Identified PRAS40 as a raptor-bound mTORC1 substrate that gates access to mTORC1's other substrates
Oshiro N.sub: Instructor in Medicine, Harvard Medical School – Xavier lab, MGH/Broad, until her death in January 2026 · Postdoc, Soukas lab, MGH & Broad Institute · Research staff, MGH/Harvard (Joseph Avruch lab) · Researcher, Kobe University (Kazuyoshi Yonezawa lab)
story: In Yonezawa's lab, Oshiro identified PRAS40 (OSH2007) as a genuine mTORC1 substrate that competes with S6K1/4E-BP1 for raptor binding.

Career crossed to Boston: Avruch lab (2013, Rag GTPase paper, published as Oshiro-Rapley), then Alexander Soukas's lab studying aging in C. elegans (2016 Cell paper on metformin/mTORC1/lifespan), then immunology/IBD in Ramnik Xavier's lab, rising to Instructor in Medicine at Harvard.

Dr. Oshiro-Rapley died on January 25, 2026, at age 51, after being struck by a snowplow vehicle while walking through a parking lot in Norwood, Massachusetts; at the time she was an Instructor in Medicine at Harvard Medical School and an investigator at the Mass General Research Institute.

highlights.HARA2002: Oshiro's lab (Yonezawa's) co-authored the founding Raptor paper.
highlights.OSH2007: PRAS40 is a raptor-bound, physiological mTORC1 substrate/inhibitor.

Liu GY.lab_name: Vance Lab, University of California, Berkeley
Liu GY.role: Wrote with David Sabatini a major 2020 review of mTOR in nutrition, growth and ageing, and in the Sabatini lab studied how mTORC1 senses nutrients such as serine
Liu GY.sub: Postdoc, Vance Lab, UC Berkeley (since 2023) · PhD, MIT Department of Biology (Sabatini lab; defended 2022) · NIH F31 fellow, mTORC1 serine sensor
story: Fifth author on GU2017 (SAMTOR discovery). Her own NIH-funded PhD project tackled how mTORC1 senses serine; led to a 2024 Nature Communications paper (with Perrimon lab, Harvard) showing flies evolved an extra sensor (Unmet) for methionine.

In 2020, alongside labwork, co-authored 'mTOR at the nexus of nutrition, growth, ageing and disease' (LIU2020) directly with David Sabatini — the field's most-cited orientation document, unusual for a graduate student to co-write.
After her PhD (Nov 2022), moved to Russell Vance's lab at UC Berkeley, studying effector-triggered immunity.

highlights.GU2017: Contributed to establishing SAMTOR as the S-adenosylmethionine sensor linking methionine metabolism to mTORC1.
highlights.LIU2020: Co-authored, with David Sabatini, the field's flagship modern review.

Condon KJ.lab_name: PhD (Sabatini lab), MIT Department of Biology
Condon KJ.role: Ran genome-wide CRISPR screens revealing how mitochondrial stress signals to mTORC1
Condon KJ.sub: Industry (Bristol Myers Squibb per a public profile, title unverified) · PhD, MIT (Sabatini lab; thesis defended March 2021) · undergrad research in enzyme chemical biology (2014–2015)
story: Fourth author on GU2017 (SAMTOR). Her own thesis (CON2021, PNAS) used genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens to catalogue mTORC1 regulators, converging on mitochondrial function: AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial distress to mTORC1 on different timescales.
Undergrad chemical biology work included collaborators like Kevan Shokat (DDX3 helicase inhibitors).
Public profile suggests move to Bristol Myers Squibb — not independently confirmed.

highlights.GU2017: Contributed to SAMTOR biochemistry as a graduate student.
highlights.CON2021: Led CRISPR screens showing AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1.

Scaria SM.lab_name: Tward Lab alumni record, UCSF Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery
Scaria SM.role: Contributed, as an MIT undergraduate in the Sabatini lab, to the discovery of CASTOR1 as the arginine sensor and SAMTOR as the SAM sensor of the mTORC1 pathway
Scaria SM.sub: UCSF medical student, continuing hearing-loss genetics research · MD/PhD, UCSF MSTP — PhD in Tward lab, UCSF Otolaryngology (2019–2022, tympanic-membrane regeneration) · BS Biological Engineering, MIT (2017; undergrad researcher, Sabatini lab)
story: As MIT undergrad, second author on CHA2016 (CASTOR1 discovery) and contributor to GU2017 (SAMTOR) in her final year — two direct amino-acid sensors before finishing her degree.
Switched fields entirely: UCSF MD/PhD, studying how the eardrum regenerates (Cell Stem Cell 2020, npj Regen Med 2023 first-author).
2025 first-author paper in Ear and Hearing on genetic-testing equity for hearing loss in underrepresented-minority children.

highlights.CHA2016: Contributed to identifying CASTOR1 as the direct arginine sensor for mTORC1.
highlights.GU2017: Contributed to identifying SAMTOR as the SAM sensor linking methionine metabolism to mTORC1.

Laplante M.lab_name: Institut universitaire de cardiologie et de pneumologie de Québec – Université Laval
Laplante M.role: Co-wrote with David Sabatini one of the field's most cited reviews of mTOR in growth and disease, and his Laval lab studies how mTORC1 and DEPTOR control fat tissue and metabolism
Laplante M.sub: Full Professor, Université Laval; Director, Research Center, CRIUCPQ · recruited to Université Laval 2011 · postdoc, Whitehead Institute, MIT (David M. Sabatini lab, 2007–2011) · PhD, Université Laval (Yves Deshaies lab, 2007)
story: As Sabatini postdoc, part of team identifying DEPTOR (PET2009) — a built-in brake on both mTOR complexes, overexpressed in some multiple myelomas to paradoxically keep Akt survival signaling on. In 2012, co-authored with Sabatini the canonical Cell review (LAP2012), still the standard reference for the field.
PhD under Yves Deshaies studying PPARγ agonists and fat redistribution.
Now directs CRIUCPQ research center, studying mTOR/DEPTOR in adipogenesis and metabolic disease.

highlights.LAP2012: Co-authors with Sabatini the field's most-cited synthesis of mTOR signaling.
highlights.PET2009: Helps identify DEPTOR as a brake on both mTOR complexes, overexpressed in some myelomas.

Laplante M.credit: Portrait: Institut universitaire de cardiologie et de pneumologie de Québec (IUCPQ) – Université Laval

Gutkind JS.lab_name: Gutkind Lab, UC San Diego Moores Cancer Center
Gutkind JS.role: Showed that persistent mTOR activation exhausts epidermal stem cells and accelerates skin ageing, and targets PI3K–mTOR signalling in head-and-neck cancer, including to make tumours respond to immunotherapy
Gutkind JS.sub: Distinguished Professor & Chair, Pharmacology, UC San Diego; Co-Director, Head and Neck Cancer Center, Moores Cancer Center · Chief, Oral and Pharyngeal Cancer Branch, NIDCR/NIH (1997–2015) · Fogarty Fellow, NIH (1986–1989) · MSc Pharmacy (1980) & MSc Biochemistry (1983), MSc/PhD Pharmacy and Biochemistry, Univ. of Buenos Aires (1985)
story: In 2009 (CAS2009), showed persistent Wnt signaling in skin switches on mTOR in epidermal stem cells, driving premature senescence — rapamycin rescued it. In 2026 (NAT2026), his UCSD team showed mTOR inhibitor everolimus reprograms the tumor microenvironment in TP53-mutant, immune-cold HNSCC — boosting T-cell/DC infiltration, cutting Tregs/MDSCs and PD-1/PD-L1.
Established that GPCRs can function as bona fide oncogenes — reshaped how the field thinks about growth-factor signaling in cancer. Led NIDCR's Oral and Pharyngeal Cancer Branch for ~2 decades.
Elected to National Academy of Medicine (2019); ACS Research Professor.

highlights.CAS2009: Wnt-induced mTOR activation drives epidermal stem-cell exhaustion; reversed by rapamycin.
highlights.NAT2026: Everolimus reprograms the TP53-mutant HNSCC immune microenvironment, restoring T-cell cytotoxicity.

Janes MR.role: Discovered that a dual TORC1/2 kinase inhibitor selectively kills leukemia cells while sparing normal lymphocytes
Janes MR.sub: Discovery scientist, Wellspring Biosciences (2011–present; KRAS G12C drug discovery) · graduate research, UC Irvine (David A. Fruman lab)
story: As grad researcher, showed PP242 (dual TORC1/2 inhibitor) kills leukemia cells while sparing normal lymphocytes (JAN2010) — unlike rapamycin. Contributed to Hsieh/Ruggero's ribosome-profiling study of oncogenic mTOR in prostate cancer (HSI2012).

Moved into industry, co-author on ARS-1620 (Cell 2018), a landmark covalent KRAS-G12C inhibitor. Still active at Wellspring on KRAS-G12C programs into 2026, including combinations with mTOR/IGF1R inhibition.

highlights.JAN2010: PP242 selectively kills leukemia cells while sparing normal lymphocytes.
highlights.HSI2012: Contributed to showing oncogenic mTOR drives prostate cancer metastasis via selective translation.

Hsieh AC.lab_name: Hsieh Lab, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle
Hsieh AC.role: Discovered that oncogenic mTOR drives cancer metastasis by selectively translating a specific pro-invasion mRNA program
Hsieh AC.sub: Professor, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center; Larry and Virginia Gordon Endowed Chair in Prostate and Bladder Cancer Research (2026) · faculty, UCSF · postdoc, UCSF (Davide Ruggero lab) · MD, Albert Einstein College of Medicine
story: As postdoc with Ruggero (who has his own medailonek), 2010 Cancer Cell paper (HSI2010) showed 4E-BP1–eIF4E, not S6 phosphorylation, mediates oncogenic mTOR signaling. His own 2012 Nature paper (HSI2012) used ribosome profiling to show mTOR selectively translates pro-invasion mRNAs in prostate cancer; INK128 reversed the signature.
Now at Fred Hutch, studying translation-driven lineage plasticity in prostate cancer (2026 JCI paper).

highlights.HSI2010: 4EBP–eIF4E axis, not S6 phosphorylation, mediates oncogenic mTOR signaling; druggable with PP242.
highlights.HSI2012: Ribosome profiling shows oncogenic mTOR selectively translates pro-invasion mRNAs driving prostate cancer metastasis.

Blagosklonny MV.role: Proposed the hyperfunction theory of ageing: TOR signalling that builds a young body never fully switches off, and drives its ageing instead
Blagosklonny MV.sub: Professor of Oncology, Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, Buffalo (2009–2024) · founding Editor-in-Chief, Cell Cycle, Aging, Oncotarget, Oncoscience · NCI, Univ. of Pennsylvania, New York Medical College, Ordway Research Institute · Fogarty Fellowship, NIH · MD & PhD, Pavlov First State Medical University, St. Petersburg · died October 2024
story: In 2009 (DEM2009), showed that blocking a cell's division while mTOR keeps driving growth tips it into permanent senescence — rapamycin uncouples growth from division, keeping arrest reversible. This anchored his 2006 theoretical paper (BLA2006) proposing the 'hyperfunction theory' of aging: growth-driving TOR signaling stays 'quasi-programmed' on past development and drives age-related disease.

Trained as a physician-scientist in Russia, moved through NIH, NCI, Penn, NYMC, Ordway before Roswell Park (2009). Founded and edited Cell Cycle, Aging, Oncotarget, Oncoscience — shaping how much of the geroscience field published for over a decade.

A polarizing, outspoken figure who publicly took rapamycin himself and advocated it for healthy people, well ahead of completed human trials — a position most of the field still treats as premature. Died October 2024 of metastatic lung cancer; over 290 peer-reviewed papers.

highlights.BLA2006: Proposes the hyperfunction theory of aging.
highlights.DEM2009: Shows the key experiment: blocking division while mTOR keeps driving growth tips cells into permanent senescence; rapamycin keeps arrest reversible.

Hoxhaj G.lab_name: Children's Medical Center Research Institute (CRI), UT Southwestern Medical Center
Hoxhaj G.role: Studies how growth signalling through PI3K, AKT and mTOR rewires cell metabolism; as a Manning-lab postdoc she co-authored work on how metformin inhibits mTORC1 in the liver
Hoxhaj G.sub: Associate Professor, UT Southwestern (since 2019) · postdoc, Brendan Manning lab, Harvard T.H. Chan School (2013–2019) · PhD, MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, Univ. of Dundee (2013) · BSc, Boğaziçi University, Istanbul
story: As Manning-lab postdoc, part of team (HOW2017) showing at low doses metformin suppresses hepatic mTORC1 specifically via AMPK and TSC complex. Co-authored with Manning a widely cited PI3K-AKT-mTOR review (HOX2019).
PhD at MRC Dundee characterizing E3 ligase ZNRF2.
Own lab since 2019, CPRIT Scholar, Pew Scholar, V Foundation Scholar, ACS Research Scholar; TAMEST Mary Beth Maddox Award 2025.

highlights.HOW2017: Metformin suppresses hepatic mTORC1 via AMPK and TSC at low doses.
highlights.HOX2019: Co-authors major review mapping PI3K-AKT-mTOR network.

Hoxhaj G.credit: Portrait: UT Southwestern, Children's Research Institute

Settembre C.lab_name: Settembre Lab, TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine), Naples
Settembre C.role: Showed that TFEB drives both autophagy and lysosome production, and that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at the lysosome to keep this program switched off when nutrients are plentiful
Settembre C.sub: Full Professor of Histology, Univ. of Naples Federico II · PI, TIGEM (since 2013) · postdoc, Columbia University & Baylor College of Medicine · PhD, University of Naples Federico II (2008, with Ballabio)
story: As first author in Ballabio's lab (SET2011), showed TFEB is the master switch turning on both autophagosome- and lysosome-building genes together. A year later (SET2012), pinned down the sensor: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB directly on the lysosome, trapping it in the cytoplasm when nutrients are abundant.

Since 2013 at TIGEM, extended the mechanism into disease: hyperactive mTORC1 in lysosomal storage disorders stunts bone growth via autophagy suppression in cartilage; more recently linked synaptic activity to TFEB-mediated tau clearance in neurodegeneration models.

highlights.SET2012: mTORC1 sits on the lysosome and phosphorylates TFEB there.
highlights.SET2011: First-authored the paper establishing TFEB as master switch for autophagy+lysosome genes.

Settembre C.credit: Portrait: TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine)

Frost M.role: Co-investigator on the EXIST-1 and EXIST-2 trials showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus shrinks tuberous sclerosis tumours in the brain and kidney
Frost M.sub: Pediatric neurologist/epileptologist, Minnesota Epilepsy Group, St. Paul, MN · child neurology fellowship, Univ. of Colorado (1977–1980) · MD, Saint Louis University (1975)
story: Sat on both pivotal EXIST trials: EXIST-1 (FRA2013) — everolimus shrank SEGA brain tumors ≥50% in 35% vs 0% placebo; EXIST-2 (BIS2013) — everolimus shrank kidney angiomyolipomas ≥50% in 42% vs 0% placebo.
Practices pediatric neurology/epilepsy at Minnesota Epilepsy Group; co-author of the 2021 International TSC Consensus Group diagnostic criteria update.

highlights.FRA2013: Site investigator on EXIST-1: everolimus shrinks SEGA brain tumors ≥50% in 35% vs 0% placebo.
highlights.BIS2013: Site investigator on EXIST-2: everolimus shrinks kidney angiomyolipomas ≥50% in 42% vs 0% placebo.

Bissler JJ.role: Led the first clinical trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus shrinks kidney angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis, and the EXIST-2 trial of everolimus for the same tumours
Bissler JJ.sub: Medical Director of Nephrology, St. Jude · Director, TSC Center of Excellence, Le Bonheur Children's Hospital · Chief, Pediatric Nephrology, Univ. of Tennessee Health Science Center · Cincinnati Children's · MD, pediatric nephrologist
story: Led the 2008 sirolimus trial (BIS2008): angiomyolipoma volume dropped to 53% of baseline by 12 months, crept back after stopping — proof mTOR blockade needs to be continuous. Key investigator on EXIST-2 (BIS2013) confirming the effect with everolimus in placebo-controlled design.
A 2023 Army-funded grant now tests whether blood-pressure drugs can prevent angiomyolipomas forming at all.

highlights.BIS2008: 24-month open-label sirolimus trial: AML volume drops to 53% of baseline, drifts back after stopping.
highlights.BIS2013: Key investigator on EXIST-2, confirming everolimus shrinks kidney AMLs in 42% vs 0% placebo.

Bissler JJ.credit: Portrait: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

Franz DN.lab_name: Tuberous Sclerosis Clinic, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center
Franz DN.role: Led the EXIST-1 trial showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus shrinks the brain tumours (SEGAs) of tuberous sclerosis, and helped run the first sirolimus trial for its kidney tumours
Franz DN.sub: Professor of Pediatrics, Univ. of Cincinnati · Founding Director, TSC Clinic, Cincinnati Children's · MD, pediatric neurologist
story: Led EXIST-1 (FRA2013, n=117): everolimus shrank SEGA brain tumors ≥50% in 35% vs 0% placebo — an alternative to high-risk neurosurgery. Collaborator on Bissler's 2008 sirolimus trial (BIS2008), groundwork for EXIST-1/2.
Founded and directs one of the longest-running, highest-volume TSC clinics in the US.

highlights.FRA2013: Led EXIST-1, proving everolimus shrinks SEGA brain tumors — cleanest randomized evidence blocking mTOR treats a genetic mTORopathy.
highlights.BIS2008: Collaborated on the earlier sirolimus trial establishing groundwork for EXIST trials.

Kapahi P.lab_name: Kapahi Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging
Kapahi P.role: Showed that reducing TOR signalling extends fruit-fly lifespan, and that the translation repressor 4E-BP is needed for dietary restriction to extend it
Kapahi P.sub: Professor, Buck Institute for Research on Aging · postdoc, Caltech (S. Benzer) · postdoc, UC San Diego (M. Karin) · PhD, Univ. of Manchester (T. Kirkwood)
story: In Benzer's lab (KAP2004), showed genetically reducing TOR pathway activity (via TSC1/TSC2, TOR, S6K) extends fly lifespan, overlapping mechanistically with dietary restriction. In 2009 (ZID2009), closed the loop: dietary restriction lowers TOR, freeing 4E-BP to selectively boost mitochondrial gene translation — required, not just correlated, for the lifespan extension.
Nathan Shock New Investigator Award (2010), NIA EUREKA Award (2010), Julie Martin Mid-Career Award (2011), Glenn Award (2015). Distinct from fellow Buck researcher Brian Kennedy.

highlights.KAP2004: Genetically dialing down TOR in Drosophila extends lifespan, overlapping with dietary restriction.
highlights.ZID2009: Dietary restriction lowers TOR, freeing 4E-BP to boost mitochondrial translation, required for lifespan extension.

Kapahi P.credit: Portrait: Buck Institute for Research on Aging

Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.lab_name: Clinical Biomarker Development, Loxo Oncology at Eli Lilly and Company (formerly Rosen Lab, Memorial Sloan Kettering)
Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.role: Showed that tumours reactivate AKT after mTOR kinase inhibition, and that the third-generation inhibitor RapaLink-1 overcomes mTOR resistance mutations
Rodrik-Outmezguine VS.sub: Associate VP, Clinical Biomarker Development, Loxo Oncology at Lilly · Precision For Medicine · Senior Scientist, Rosen Lab, MSKCC · PhD
story: Led ROD2011 (Cancer Discovery): mTOR-kinase inhibitors trigger a biphasic AKT rebound via feedback release of upstream RTK signaling. Led follow-up ROD2016 (Nature, with Shokat's chemistry group): RapaLink-1, a bivalent third-gen inhibitor bridging mTOR's two drug pockets, overcomes resistance mutations.
Moved from academic pharmacology into translational/clinical biomarker science, now at Loxo Oncology/Lilly designing biomarker strategy for precision-oncology trials.

highlights.ROD2011: mTOR-kinase inhibitors trigger feedback-dependent biphasic AKT rebound.
highlights.ROD2016: RapaLink-1 overcomes resistance mutations that defeat first/second-gen mTOR inhibitors.

Rosen N.lab_name: Rosen Lab (Member Emeritus), Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Rosen N.role: Showed that blocking mTORC1 releases a feedback brake on receptor tyrosine kinases and AKT, explaining how tumours escape mTOR and PI3K inhibitors and shaping how these drugs are combined in the clinic
Rosen N.sub: Member Emeritus, MSKCC · fellowship, NCI · residency, Brigham and Women's Hospital · MD, PhD, Albert Einstein College of Medicine
story: In 2006 (ORE2006), showed mTOR inhibition paradoxically activates upstream RTK/Akt signaling via feedback release — foundational explanation for why single-agent mTOR inhibitors often fail. As senior author on ROD2011, extended this to mTOR-kinase inhibitors.
This 'feedback reactivation' framework became a central organizing principle of modern targeted-therapy combinations. NIH/NCI Outstanding Investigator Award (2016); AACR Academy Fellow (2022).

highlights.ORE2006: mTOR inhibition relieves feedback suppression of RTK signaling, paradoxically activating Akt.
highlights.ROD2011: Senior author: mTOR-kinase inhibitors cause feedback-dependent biphasic AKT rebound.

Rosen N.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Grabiner BC.role: Catalogued cancer-associated MTOR mutations and showed that many of them hyperactivate the kinase and can predict sensitivity to rapamycin; he also contributed to the discovery of GATOR1
Grabiner BC.sub: Senior Principal Scientist, Valo Health · Biogen · MIT Dept. of Biology · Whitehead Institute
story: Helped identify GATOR1 (BAR2013) — a GAP for the Rag GTPases; mutated in cancers, making tumors hypersensitive to rapamycin. Led follow-up (GRA2014) cataloguing cancer-associated MTOR mutations that hyperactivate the kinase and predict rapamycin sensitivity.
Moved into industry: Biogen (lipid transport, Alzheimer's biology), now Valo Health (AI-driven drug discovery).

highlights.BAR2013: GATOR1 is a GAP shutting Rag GTPases (and mTORC1) off when amino acids run low.
highlights.GRA2014: Cancer-associated MTOR mutations are hyperactivating and predict rapamycin sensitivity.

Guri Y.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel
Guri Y.role: Showed mTORC2 drives liver cancer by rewiring lipid and sphingolipid synthesis
Guri Y.sub: Investigator, Botnar Research Centre for Child Health (BRCCH) · University Hospital Basel (Internal Medicine) · MD-PhD, Biozentrum, Univ. of Basel (Hall lab)
story: In a fatty-liver-to-HCC mouse model, showed mTORC2 drives tumor formation by ramping up de novo lipid/sphingolipid synthesis (GUR2017); blocking synthesis prevented tumors. Co-authored a review (GUR2016) on mTOR as a resistance mechanism against targeted cancer drugs.
MD-PhD; returned to clinical medicine at University Hospital Basel (treated COVID-19 patients), now also affiliated with BRCCH.

highlights.GUR2017: mTORC2 promotes tumorigenesis via de novo lipid synthesis.
highlights.GUR2016: Review of mTOR signaling conferring resistance to targeted cancer drugs.

Guri Y.credit: Portrait: Botnar Research Centre for Child Health (BRCCH)

Loewith R.role: Discovered that TOR exists as two distinct complexes, founding the TORC1/TORC2 framework
Loewith R.sub: Professor, Univ. of Geneva (since 2005) · postdoc, Univ. of Basel (Michael N. Hall) · PhD, Univ. of Calgary (Dallan Young) · BSc, Univ. of Guelph
story: As Hall-lab postdoc, showed (LOE2002) TOR assembles into two biochemically distinct complexes — TORC1 (rapamycin-sensitive) and TORC2 (insensitive, controls actin polarity) — founding the field's organizing vocabulary. In 2009 (FEL2009), helped test the first ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors (TORKinibs) against this two-complex model.
Own lab at Univ. of Geneva since 2005; ERC Starting (2008) and Consolidator (2014) grants; Deputy Director, NCCR Chemical Biology; elected EMBO Member.

highlights.LOE2002: Defines TORC1/TORC2 as biochemically distinct complexes, founding the two-complex paradigm.
highlights.FEL2009: Helped test the first ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors (TORKinibs) against both complexes.

Yang H.lab_name: Pavletich Lab, Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Yang H.role: Solved, as first author in the Pavletich lab, the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase and the structure of mTORC1 activated by RHEB
Yang H.sub: Senior Research Scientist, Structural Biology Program, MSKCC (Pavletich Lab)
story: First author on the 2013 crystal structure of the mTOR kinase (YAN2013), revealing the FRB 'gatekeeper' domain. First author again in 2017 (YAN2017) on cryo-EM/crystal structures of intact mTORC1 bound to RHEB and PRAS40, revealing the allosteric activation/inhibition mechanism.
Both studies from Nikola Pavletich's lab (who has his own medailonek in the Atlas).

highlights.YAN2013: Solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, revealing the FRB gatekeeper domain.
highlights.YAN2017: Solved structures of mTORC1 bound to RHEB/PRAS40, revealing the allosteric activation mechanism.

Yang H.credit: Portrait: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

Chen C.lab_name: The Chen-Liu Lab, State Key Laboratory of Biotherapy, West China Hospital, Sichuan University
Chen C.role: Showed that blood stem cells need TSC to keep mTOR in check in order to stay dormant and self-renew, and that rapamycin restores the function of aged blood stem cells in mice
Chen C.sub: Professor, West China Hospital, Sichuan University · postdoc, Scott Lowe lab, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory & MSKCC · PhD, University of Michigan
story: First author (CHE2008): deleting Tsc1 (unleashing mTOR) drove resting blood stem cells into rapid division, flooded them with ROS, destroyed regenerative capacity — antioxidant partly rescued them. Follow-up (CHE2009): mTOR rises naturally in aged HSCs, and rapamycin restores regenerative capacity and vaccine response.
Postdoc'd with Scott Lowe (lineage plasticity/therapy resistance), now co-runs a lab with Yu (Kiki) Liu (co-author on both original papers) studying epigenetic reprogramming in cancer.

highlights.CHE2008: Deleting Tsc1 drives blood stem cells into rapid division, ROS flood, and exhausts self-renewal.
highlights.CHE2009: mTOR rises in aged HSCs; rapamycin restores their regenerative function and vaccine response.

Chen C.credit: Portrait: West China Hospital, Sichuan University

Zheng P.role: Showed as senior author that blood stem cells need TSC to keep mTOR in check in order to stay dormant, and that rapamycin restores the function of aged blood stem cells in mice
Zheng P.sub: Co-founder & CMO, OncoC4, Inc. · Professor, Univ. of Michigan, Ohio State, Children's National, Univ. of Maryland IHV · PhD, Yale · MD, Peking Union Medical College
story: Senior author on both CHE2008 and CHE2009 (HSC aging/mTOR). Long partnership with immunologist Yang Liu spanning Yale, Ohio State, Michigan, Children's National, Univ. of Maryland IHV; co-discovered the CD24–Siglec-10 checkpoint, translated into CD24Fc (tested for GVHD and severe COVID).
Co-founded OncoC4 (formerly OncoImmune), where he's now CMO directing global checkpoint-immunotherapy trials.

highlights.CHE2008: Senior author: TSC-mTOR keeps blood stem cells quiescent by repressing mitochondrial ROS.
highlights.CHE2009: Senior author: mTOR hyperactivation drives HSC aging; rapamycin restores function and immune competence.

Viollet B.role: Showed that metformin still lowers liver glucose production without AMPK or LKB1, pointing instead to a drop in cellular energy charge
Viollet B.sub: Directeur de Recherche (INSERM), Institut Cochin · shifted to AMPK biology late 1990s · trained in Axel Kahn's lab, Institut Cochin de Génétique Moléculaire
story: In 2010 (FOR2010), using AMPK/LKB1-knockout mice and hepatocytes, showed metformin still suppresses hepatic glucose production — contradicting the standard AMPK-dependent model, pointing instead to a drop in energy charge. His AMPK-knockout genetic tools were what let the 2011 ULK1 study (KIM2011) cleanly separate AMPK's activating vs. mTORC1's inhibitory phosphorylation of ULK1.

Began career in liver gene transcription (Axel Kahn lab), then built AMPK-subunit knockout mouse lines used field-wide for two decades. Nutrition Research Award (2000), Institut Benjamin Delessert Prize (2004), Descartes-Huygens Prize (2015).

highlights.KIM2011: Contributes AMPK-knockout genetic tools letting the study cleanly show AMPK/mTORC1's opposing regulation of ULK1.
highlights.FOR2010: Metformin still suppresses hepatic glucose production without AMPK or LKB1.

Kim J.role: Showed as a Guan-lab postdoc that AMPK and mTORC1 control autophagy by phosphorylating ULK1 at different sites, with mTORC1's mark on Ser757 blocking activation by AMPK
Kim J.sub: Professor, Dept. of Oral Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Kyung Hee University, Seoul · training/postdoc in Kun-Liang Guan's lab, Univ. of Michigan Life Sciences Institute → UC San Diego
story: First author (KIM2011): AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1 at activating sites, mTORC1 phosphorylates Ser757 to keep it off and block AMPK access — the tug-of-war deciding autophagy on/off. Co-authored with Guan an influential 2019 review (KIM2019) reframing mTOR as the central hub of nutrient signaling.

Long apprenticeship in Guan's lab (Michigan → UCSD). Now Professor at Kyung Hee dental school, Seoul — extending AMPK/mTOR/autophagy biology into oral/dental contexts, retains UCSD Pharmacology affiliation.

highlights.KIM2011: First author: mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 at Ser757 to keep autophagy off and block AMPK's activating site.
highlights.KIM2019: Co-authors influential review reframing mTOR as the central hub integrating nutrient signals with cell growth.

Demetriades C.lab_name: Max Planck Research Group Demetriades, Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing, Cologne
Demetriades C.role: Showed as a postdoc in Aurelio Teleman's lab that starvation and other stresses pull TSC2 to the lysosome to switch mTORC1 off. His Max Planck group in Cologne studies how cells sense nutrients and stress through mTORC1 and how this changes with age
Demetriades C.sub: Max Planck Research Group Leader, MPI for Biology of Ageing, Cologne (since 2017) · postdoc, DKFZ Heidelberg (Aurelio Teleman lab, 2010–2016) · PhD, BSRC 'Alexander Fleming' & Aristotle Univ. (George Mosialos lab, 2003–2009) · BSc, Aristotle Univ. of Thessaloniki (2003)
story: As Teleman-lab postdoc, showed (DEM2014) starvation pulls TSC2 onto the lysosome to directly switch off Rheb/mTORC1 — the missing piece beyond Rag-GTPase relocation. Follow-up (DEM2016): many stress types (energy, hypoxia, osmotic, oxidative, growth-factor withdrawal) independently drive TSC2 to the lysosome — a general damage-control mechanism.

Own MPI-AGE group since 2017 (ERC Starting Grant), continuing to dissect the spatial logic of mTORC1 signaling (2024: mTORC1 does different jobs at different locations). FEBS Young Scientists' Fellowship (2014), Walther Flemming Award (2019).

highlights.DEM2014: Amino-acid starvation recruits TSC2 to the lysosome to inactivate Rheb and mTORC1.
highlights.DEM2016: Lysosomal TSC2 recruitment is a universal response to many cellular stresses.

Demetriades C.credit: Portrait: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing

Teleman AA.lab_name: Division of Signal Transduction in Cancer and Metabolism, DKFZ, Heidelberg
Teleman AA.role: Uses fruit-fly genetics and human cells to study how growth signalling through TOR controls cell and body size. His lab showed that starvation and other stresses move TSC2 to the lysosome to switch mTORC1 off
Teleman AA.sub: Division Head, DKFZ (since 2012) · Junior Group Leader, DKFZ (2007) · McKinsey & Co. (2001–2002) · PhD, EMBL & Imperial College London (Stephen M. Cohen, 2004) · AB Biochemistry, Harvard (Richard Losick, 1998) · EMBO Member (2020)

Trained as biochemist at Harvard, PhD with Stephen Cohen (fly growth signaling), briefly a McKinsey consultant. ERC Starting/Consolidator/Advanced grants.

highlights.DEM2014: Senior author: amino-acid starvation recruits TSC2 to the lysosome to inhibit Rheb and mTORC1.
highlights.DEM2016: Senior author: lysosomal TSC2 recruitment triggered by many cellular stresses, a general damage-control mechanism.

Markhard AL.lab_name: Long Lab, Stanford (formerly Mootha Lab, Broad/MGH)
Markhard AL.role: Contributed, as a Sabatini-lab researcher, to the discovery that Ragulator docks mTORC1 on the lysosome, and now studies metabolite signals that tell the body it has eaten
Markhard AL.sub: Ph.D. student, NYU Grossman School of Medicine · Research Scientist, Long Lab, Stanford · Lab Manager, Mootha Lab, Broad/MGH (2012–2022) · Research staff, Sabatini Lab, Whitehead/MIT
story: Part of team showing (SAR2006) prolonged rapamycin also disassembles mTORC2, root of insulin-resistance side effect. Part of team (SAN2010) showing Ragulator recruits Rag GTPases to the lysosomal surface, docking mTORC1 next to Rheb.

Decade as Mootha-lab manager mapping mitochondrial proteins, then Stanford metabolomics (2024 Nature: enzyme PTER/taurine; 2026 Nature Metabolism: python-derived gut-brain feeding signal). Now pursuing a PhD at NYU.

highlights.SAR2006: Co-authored: prolonged rapamycin disassembles mTORC2, explaining the insulin-resistance side effect.
highlights.SAN2010: Helped show Ragulator recruits Rag GTPases to the lysosomal surface, docking mTORC1 next to Rheb.

Hsu PP.lab_name: Hsu Lab, University of Michigan Rogel Cancer Center
Hsu PP.role: Identified Grb10 as an mTORC1 substrate that feeds back to dampen insulin and growth-factor signalling, and now studies the earliest steps of lung cancer as a physician-scientist
Hsu PP.sub: University of Michigan · postdoc, Vander Heiden Lab, MIT · oncology fellowship, Dana-Farber & MGH · residency, Brigham and Women's · MD, Harvard · PhD, MIT (Sabatini Lab) · BA, Princeton
story: Used quantitative phosphoproteomics (HSU2011) to map mTOR's substrates directly, identifying Grb10 — mTORC1 phosphorylates/stabilizes it, and Grb10 suppresses PI3K/growth-factor signaling, explaining mTORC1-hyperactivation-causes-insulin-resistance.
