Physician-scientist path through MIT/Harvard/Dana-Farber/MGH; now thoracic oncologist and stem cell biologist studying how airway basal cells give rise to never-smoking, ALK-fusion lung cancer. NCI K08, Burroughs Wellcome Fund Career Award (2025), 2026 ASCI Young Physician-Scientist.

highlights.HSU2011: Mapped the mTOR phosphoproteome, identifying Grb10 as a direct mTORC1 substrate feeding back on PI3K.

Hsu PP.credit: Portrait: American Society for Clinical Investigation (ASCI)

Sengupta S.role: Showed that mTORC1 controls whether the liver makes ketone bodies during fasting, and now leads biology for drug discovery at a metabolic-disease biotech
Sengupta S.sub: SVP, Head of Biology, Atavistik Bio · Associate Director, Agios · Lead Biologist, Navitor Pharmaceuticals · Broad Institute CDoT · Catabasis Pharmaceuticals · postdoc, Brugge Lab, Harvard Medical School · PhD, Whitehead/MIT (Sabatini Lab)
story: Showed (SEN2010) that during fasting the liver must switch mTORC1 off to make ketones — losing TSC1 locked the pathway on and blocked ketogenesis via PPARα/NCoR1; aged livers show chronically elevated mTORC1 and a similar ketogenesis defect.
Moved through Catabasis, Broad CDoT, Navitor (built on Sabatini-lab amino-acid-sensing biology), Agios, now heading biology at Atavistik Bio's metabolism pipeline.

highlights.SEN2010: mTORC1 suppresses fasting-induced hepatic ketogenesis via PPARα; suppression worsens with age.

Ehninger D.role: Showed that rapamycin reverses learning deficits in adult mice carrying a tuberous sclerosis mutation, and later tested carefully whether rapamycin's lifespan effect reflects a true slowing of ageing
Ehninger D.sub: Group Leader, DZNE Bonn (since 2010) · postdoc, UCLA (Alcino Silva lab, 2004–2009) · MD, Charité Berlin/UCL/Mount Sinai/Harvard (clinical training)
story: As UCLA postdoc, showed (EHN2008) Tsc2+/- mice have hyperactive mTOR/hippocampal learning deficits, reversible with a short rapamycin course — an early demonstration mTOR drugs could treat cognitive symptoms of a genetic disorder. At DZNE, led a rigorous large-scale phenotyping study (NEF2013): rapamycin extends mouse lifespan but leaves most classic aging phenotypes unchanged — a standard citation distinguishing 'longer life' from 'slower aging.'
Physician trained in neurology before full-time research; DZNE group continues skeptical, rigorous mouse-aging science.

highlights.EHN2008: Rapamycin reverses hippocampal learning/memory deficits in Tsc2+/- mice.
highlights.NEF2013: Rapamycin extends lifespan but leaves most classic aging markers unchanged.

Egan DF.lab_name: Shaw Lab, Salk Institute (where this work was done)
Egan DF.role: Showed as first author that AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1, linking low cellular energy to autophagy and mitophagy, and contributed to the finding that AMPK brakes mTORC1 by phosphorylating raptor
Egan DF.sub: Director, Eli Lilly · industry: Orna Therapeutics, ReNAgade Therapeutics, Casma Therapeutics · postdoc, Harvard Medical School (2014–2018) · PhD, UCSD/Salk (Reuben Shaw lab, 2008–2014) · BA, Colby College
story: Co-author (GWI2008): AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor, a second route (beyond TSC2) to shut mTORC1 down during energy stress. First author (EGA2010): AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1, connecting energy sensing to mitophagy.
Moved from Salk PhD through Harvard postdoc into a string of Boston biotechs, now a director at Eli Lilly — an academic-to-industry path shaping AMPK/autophagy drug discovery.

highlights.GWI2008: AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor, a second route to shut down mTORC1 during energy stress.
highlights.EGA2010: AMPK directly phosphorylates ULK1, linking energy sensing to mitophagy.

Wyant GA.lab_name: Wyant Lab, MGH Cardiovascular Research Center
Wyant GA.role: Showed that the lysosomal protein SLC38A9 exports leucine and other essential amino acids out of the lysosome, letting cells grow on proteins they have taken up and broken down there
Wyant GA.sub: Assistant Professor, MGH/Harvard Medical School · postdoc, Dana-Farber (William Kaelin lab) · PhD, MIT/Whitehead (Sabatini lab) · BS, Northeastern Univ.
story: First author (WYA2017): SLC38A9, already known for arginine sensing, has a second job — effluxing essential amino acids like leucine out of lysosomes to activate mTORC1; pancreatic cancer cells scavenging protein by macropinocytosis depend on this efflux. Pivoted to oxygen sensing with Nobel laureate William Kaelin, now runs own MGH/Harvard lab studying oxygen, nutrients, mechanical stretch and electrical activity in heart/muscle growth — aimed at heart failure and cachexia.

highlights.WYA2017: SLC38A9 effluxes essential amino acids out of lysosomes to activate mTORC1.
highlights.CHA2016: Contributed to identifying CASTOR1 as the direct arginine sensor upstream of mTORC1.

Rogala KB.role: Solved the atomic-resolution structures that show how mTORC1 physically docks and gets switched on at the lysosome
Rogala KB.sub: Assistant Professor, Stanford (Structural Biology & Chemical & Systems Biology) · postdoc, MIT/Whitehead (Sabatini lab) · DPhil, Univ. of Oxford · MRes, UCL · BSc, Univ. of Edinburgh
story: First author (ROG2019, Science): cryo-EM at 3.2 Å of Raptor bound to Rag-Ragulator, revealing how mTORC1 reads the Rag GTPases' nucleotide state to dock at the lysosome. Co-first author (VAL2022, Nature): GATOR2's cryo-EM structure — a 1.1 MDa, two-fold symmetric cage with octagonal scaffold and 8 paired WD40 propellers, mapping Sestrin2/CASTOR1 docking sites.
Now leads his own Stanford lab, studying 'cellular intelligence' — how cells sense nutrients and growth signals — with an eye toward cancer and tuberous sclerosis therapeutics.

highlights.ROG2019: Cryo-EM shows how Raptor reads Rag GTPase nucleotide states to dock mTORC1 at the lysosome.
highlights.VAL2022: Co-first author: cryo-EM structure of GATOR2, mapping Sestrin2/CASTOR1 docking.

Yu Yonghao.lab_name: Yu Lab, Columbia University Irving Medical Center
Yu Yonghao.role: Used phosphoproteomics to show that mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises Grb10, which then acts as a feedback brake on insulin and IGF-1 signalling
Yu Yonghao.sub: Professor, Columbia University Irving Medical Center · Associate Professor, UT Southwestern · postdoc, Harvard Medical School (Steven Gygi & John Blenis) · PhD Chemistry, UC Berkeley (Julie Leary) · BS Chemistry, Fudan Univ.

highlights.YUX2011: Phosphoproteomics identify Grb10 as a direct mTORC1 substrate creating negative feedback on insulin/PI3K signaling.

Ferguson SM.lab_name: Ferguson Lab, Yale School of Medicine
Ferguson SM.role: Showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to keep the lysosome-building program switched off, and that folliculin is required at the lysosome for amino acids to recruit and activate mTORC1

story: Showed (ROC2012) mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (Ser211), recruiting 14-3-3 to trap it in the cytoplasm — independent, complementary work to the Settembre/Ballabio TFEB papers. Jiaqiang Jiang.lab_name: Department of General Surgery & Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University
Jiaqiang Jiang.role: Member of the Nanfang Hospital gastric-cancer surgery team that traced how a tumor-enriched gut bacterium rewires CD8+ T cells through an mTOR-linked checkpoint to blunt anti-PD-1 therapy.
Jiaqiang Jiang.sub: Department of General Surgery · Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor · Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University · Guangzhou, China
story: Jiaqiang Jiang works in the gastrointestinal-tumor surgery group at Nanfang Hospital (Southern Medical University, Guangzhou) led by Yanfeng Hu. In the study behind this entry, the team found that the bacterium Streptococcus anginosus is enriched in gastric tumors that fail to respond to PD-1 checkpoint blockade, and that it produces a metabolite, kynurenic acid, which pushes up integrin α2 (ITGA2) on CD8+ T cells. ITGA2 in turn dampens an mTOR-dependent signaling step, keeping cathepsin V high and interferon-γ/granzyme B output low — effectively disarming the cytotoxic T cells the immunotherapy needs to work. Blocking ITGA2 restored T-cell killing activity and resensitized tumors to PD-1 blockade.

This is Jiang's only study currently in the Atlas under this name. PubMed shows the same Jiang, with the identical Nanfang Hospital affiliation, as a co-author on at least two other 2026 papers from the same lab on gut-microbiota–immune crosstalk in gastrointestinal cancers, suggesting a working researcher embedded in this specific research line rather than a one-off contributor.

highlights.REN2026: Co-author on the Nanfang Hospital team that identified the Streptococcus anginosus–kynurenic acid–ITGA2–mTOR–cathepsin V axis driving PD-1 blockade resistance in gastric cancer.

Yukun Zhang.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Yukun Zhang.role: Senior author of a study showing that failing chaperone-mediated autophagy lets midnolin accumulate and degrade TSC2, overactivating mTORC1 and accelerating intervertebral disc degeneration
Yukun Zhang.sub: Department of Orthopedics · Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College · Huazhong University of Science and Technology · Wuhan, China
story: Yukun Zhang is a corresponding/senior author in the spine research group at Union Hospital, Wuhan. The team showed that in degenerating intervertebral discs, a quality-control pathway (chaperone-mediated autophagy) fails, letting the protein Midnolin (MIDN) pile up; accumulated MIDN then binds and destroys TSC2, the brake on mTORC1. With that brake gone, mTORC1 hyperactivates, pushing disc cells into senescence and breaking down the disc's extracellular matrix. Restoring autophagy, removing MIDN, or directly inhibiting mTORC1 with rapamycin each reversed the damage.

PubMed lists Zhang as corresponding author on multiple other 2026 Union Hospital papers on disc-degeneration biomaterials and cell therapy, indicating Zhang leads this hospital's intervertebral-disc-degeneration research line.

Qingsong Liu.lab_name: Qingsong Liu Lab, Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Qingsong Liu.role: Medicinal chemist in Nathanael Gray's lab who helped discover Torin1, an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, and later built an independent kinase-inhibitor drug-discovery program in China
Qingsong Liu.sub: PI, Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences – formerly Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School (Gray lab)
story: In 2009, Qingsong Liu was a medicinal chemist in Nathanael Gray's lab (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute / Harvard Medical School) and co-authored the Thoreen et al. paper reporting Torin1 — the first highly potent, selective ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor. The result reshaped the field: rapamycin only partially suppresses mTORC1, whereas directly blocking the kinase's ATP site with Torin1 hits those 'rapamycin-resistant' functions too — motivating a whole generation of second-generation mTOR kinase inhibitors.

Liu went on to lead his own kinase-inhibitor medicinal chemistry program at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, developing the 'CHMFL' series of inhibitors against FLT3, BCR-ABL, EGFR, c-KIT, RIPK1 and other kinases for leukemia, GIST and inflammatory disease. The institutional trail (Harvard/Dana-Farber → Hefei CAS) and unbroken focus on ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor chemistry make this identification highly likely, though not formally confirmed in a single source.

highlights.THO2009: As a chemist in Nathanael Gray's lab, contributed to the discovery and characterization of Torin1, the first potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, establishing that direct mTOR kinase inhibition blocks rapamycin-resistant functions of mTORC1.

Qianqian Liu.role: Biostatistician on one of the first randomised pilot trials of rapamycin's safety in older adults
Qianqian Liu.sub: Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics · UT Health San Antonio, USA
story: Qianqian Liu contributed biostatistical work to the 2018 Kraig et al. paper — one of the earliest placebo-controlled human pilot trials testing whether low-dose rapamycin (1 mg/day) is safe and tolerable in healthy older adults (70-95 years old), run out of UT Health San Antonio's Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies.

Sunghoon Kim.role: Senior author of the 2012 study proposing leucyl-tRNA synthetase as an intracellular leucine sensor for mTORC1, part of his broader work on the signalling roles of tRNA synthetases

story: Sunghoon Kim is one of the most decorated biochemists in South Korea. He is the senior/corresponding author of Han JM et al., Cell 2012, which solved a long-standing puzzle: how cells directly sense intracellular leucine levels to switch on mTORC1. His group showed that leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LRS) — an enzyme whose textbook job is attaching leucine to its tRNA for protein synthesis — moonlights as a leucine sensor, binding the Rag GTPase in a leucine-dependent manner and acting as its GAP to trigger mTORC1 activation.

That discovery sits inside a decades-long research program: PhD at Brown University (1991), postdoctoral work at MIT, and a career at Seoul National University since 2001, directing a sequence of national research centers on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases — most recently the Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center. His lab discovered that several tRNA synthetases act as tumor suppressors, establishing them as a genuinely new class of signaling molecules in human disease. He has received Korea's Top Scientist and Technologist Award (2006), the Korean National Academy of Science Award (2012), and the Ho-Am Prize in Medicine (2015) — often described as Korea's answer to the Nobel Prize.

highlights.HAN2012: Senior/corresponding author establishing leucyl-tRNA synthetase as the intracellular leucine sensor that activates mTORC1 — a foundational mTOR nutrient-sensing discovery.

That work culminated in the paper flagged here: 'mTORC1, the maestro of cell metabolism and growth' (Genes & Development, 2025), where she is listed first and shares the corresponding-author line with Blenis himself — an unusual arrangement for a field-defining review, signaling she is effectively the lab's senior authority on mTORC1 metabolic biology.

story: Yanhui Xu is a professor at Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and one of China's most prominent structural biologists, using cryo-EM and biochemistry to determine how large multi-protein machines assemble and function.

On mTOR specifically, his lab produced the field's first cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1 (2016) and then, in the 2018 Cell Research paper verified here, the first cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 — revealing a hollow, two-fold-symmetric dimer in which Rictor and mSin1 sterically block FKBP12-rapamycin from binding mTOR, explaining mTORC2's relative rapamycin insensitivity compared with mTORC1.

His earlier work solved structures underlying DNA methylation, and since 2020 his group has published four papers in Science resolving the complete transcription pre-initiation complex — work named one of 'China's Top 10 Advances in Life Sciences' for 2021, and for which he received the 2021 Xplorer Prize from the Tencent Foundation.

story: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare, locally aggressive vascular tumor of infancy. Sirolimus, which blocks mTOR, is the standard drug for KHE, but doctors did not know whether tumor location changes how well it responds.

story: Before 2008, scientists knew amino acids switch on mTORC1 but not how that signal physically reached the enzyme. In 2008, two labs independently cracked this in the same month: Yenal Sancak in David Sabatini's lab (Science), and Eunjung Kim in Kun-Liang Guan's lab (Nature Cell Biology), both showed that Rag GTPases sense amino acids and physically recruit mTORC1 to the lysosome surface, where it gets switched on. Kim was first author on the Guan lab's paper, built largely on Drosophila genetics and mammalian cell experiments — now textbook mTOR biology.

Kim appears as a co-author on two other Guan-lab papers from the same period, indicating she continued in the lab for at least a couple more years. Her subsequent career could not be reliably traced — 'Eunjung Kim' is a very common Korean name and no confidently-matched later publication record was found.

highlights.KIM2008: First author on the 2008 discovery that Rag GTPases activate TORC1 in response to amino acids — one of two simultaneous, independent 2008 papers that established the amino-acid-sensing arm of the mTOR pathway.

Eunjoon Kim.lab_name: Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions, Institute for Basic Science & Department of Biological Sciences, KAIST
Eunjoon Kim.role: Neuroscientist who directs the IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions and studies synaptic scaffold proteins linked to autism; he contributed to work linking neuronal ERBB4 and mTOR signalling to Alzheimer's pathology
Eunjoon Kim.sub: Professor, KAIST Department of Biological Sciences · Director, IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions · &gt;200 papers · Asan Award in Medicine (2018), POSCO TJ Park Prize (2013)
story: Eunjoon Kim built his career mapping the molecular architecture of the synapse — in particular the SHANK family of postsynaptic scaffold proteins, whose mutations are among the best-established genetic causes of autism spectrum disorder. He now directs the IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions at KAIST, with over 200 papers published.

In this 2026 Nature paper from Won-Suk Chung's group (also at KAIST/IBS), Kim is a senior co-author on work showing that aberrant ERBB4 expression in excitatory neurons drives synapse loss, amyloid deposition, and cognitive decline via mTOR signaling — connecting his long-standing expertise in synaptic biology to the molecular front lines of neurodegeneration.

highlights.LEE2026: Senior co-author (director, IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions; KAIST) on a 2026 Nature study showing aberrant ERBB4 expression in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like synapse loss and pathology via mTOR signaling.

Eunjoon Kim.credit: Portrait: IBS Center for Synaptic Brain Dysfunctions

Shiwen Chen.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology & Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University
Shiwen Chen.role: Aquaculture physiologist studying why the largemouth bass, a carnivorous fish, tolerates dietary carbohydrate so poorly
Shiwen Chen.sub: Aquaculture nutrition researcher · Shanghai Ocean University
story: Chen and colleagues compared largemouth bass with tilapia on graded-carbohydrate diets and traced bass's poor carbohydrate tolerance to a blunted insulin → AKT1 → mTOR → SREBP1 signaling axis. Using gene knockdown in bass liver cells, the team showed the chain of command directly: silencing akt1 or s6k1 blocked SREBP1 activation, silencing tsc2 restored mTOR signaling, and blocking mTOR with rapamycin reproduced the glycogen-overload phenotype.

highlights.TAO2026: Second author on a comparative fish physiology study showing largemouth bass have a blunted insulin/AKT1/mTOR/SREBP1 axis that diverts excess dietary carbohydrate into liver glycogen rather than fat.

Sheng Chen.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Sheng Chen.role: Orthopaedic researcher who contributed to a study showing that the plant compound corilagin protects joint cartilage by calming inflammation and restoring autophagy
Sheng Chen.sub: Orthopedic surgeon-researcher · Tongji Hospital, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan
story: In inflamed mouse chondrocytes and a surgical osteoarthritis model, the plant compound corilagin reduced cartilage-degrading enzymes, restored markers of healthy cartilage, and dialed down both NF-κB signaling and overactive PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling — which let autophagy resume. Blocking autophagy chemically partly undid corilagin's benefit, confirming autophagy restoration as part of the mechanism.

highlights.ZHOU2026B: Co-author on a preclinical study showing the plant compound corilagin protects cartilage in an osteoarthritis model by blocking NF-κB inflammatory signaling and PI3K/AKT/mTOR overactivation, restoring chondrocytes' protective autophagy.

Yunwei Wang.lab_name: Department of Burn Plastic and Wound Repair Surgery, The Second Hospital of Lanzhou University
Yunwei Wang.role: Burn and wound-repair researcher who contributed to a study testing the plant flavonoid dihydromyricetin as an anti-scarring treatment
Yunwei Wang.sub: Burn & wound-repair surgery researcher · The Second Hospital of Lanzhou University
story: Wang and colleagues tested dihydromyricetin (a flavonoid found in vine tea) on hypertrophic scars. In scar-derived fibroblasts, it lowered fibrosis markers alongside reduced PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activity, and in a rabbit-ear hypertrophic scar model, it visibly improved scar appearance and reduced collagen buildup.

highlights.CAO2026B: Co-author on a study combining network pharmacology with lab experiments to show dihydromyricetin reduces fibrosis markers in hypertrophic scar tissue alongside decreased PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activity, replicated in a rabbit-ear scar model.

Yifei Wang.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Pesticide & Chemical Biology (Ministry of Education) & Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, Central China Normal University
Yifei Wang.role: Environmental toxicologist who contributed to a study of how early-life exposure to food-contact microplastics and a common plasticiser disrupts brain development through mTOR signalling
Yifei Wang.sub: Environmental toxicology researcher · Central China Normal University, Wuhan
story: Exposed young mice showed autism-relevant behavioral changes alongside neuronal damage in the prefrontal cortex and reduced expression of two autism-risk genes. Proteomic screening pointed to the mTOR pathway as the central mechanism: exposure over-activated mTOR signaling, impairing autophagy and disrupting synapse-plasticity genes. Treating mice with rapamycin reversed both the autophagy impairment and most of the behavioral changes.

highlights.YANG2026: Co-author on a toxicology study in young mice showing combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP produces autism-relevant behavioral changes via mTOR pathway overactivation and impaired autophagy — reversed by the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin.

Joy Zhao.lab_name: Cregan Laboratory, Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario
Joy Zhao.role: Researcher in Sean Cregan's lab studying how chronic cell-stress signalling through ATF4 suppresses mTOR and kills dopamine neurons in Parkinson's disease models
Joy Zhao.sub: Research staff/trainee, Cregan lab · Robarts Research Institute, Western University, London, Canada
story: Working in Parkinson's disease models, the Cregan lab found that sustained activity of the stress-response transcription factor ATF4 turns on a set of genes whose combined effect is to chronically suppress both mTORC1 and mTORC2. That suppression helps activate a pro-death protein, pushing dopamine-producing neurons toward death — identifying a maladaptive 'ATF4-mTOR' axis as a potential new drug target for slowing neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: Co-author on a mechanistic study identifying a maladaptive ATF4-mTOR signaling axis — chronic integrated-stress-response activation suppresses both mTORC1 and mTORC2, triggering dopaminergic neuron death in Parkinson's disease models.

Jiaqi Zhao.lab_name: Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis & State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech)
Jiaqi Zhao.role: Co-author; chemical biologist who helped build a chemical probe revealing a glycolytic enzyme's secret second job as a methionine sensor for mTORC1.
Jiaqi Zhao.sub: Chemical biology researcher · Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Shenzhen
story: To find the cell's methionine sensor directly, Zhao and colleagues built a 'Trojan horse' chemical probe: a photoaffinity version of methionine that tags whatever protein grabs onto it when hit with light. That fishing expedition landed on PKM2 — an enzyme best known for its day job in glucose metabolism — which the team showed binds methionine through a newly identified pocket and relays that signal through GATOR2 to control mTORC1.

highlights.SANG2026: Co-author on a chemical-biology study using a photoaffinity methionine probe to identify PKM2 as a direct methionine-sensing protein that signals through the GATOR2 complex to regulate mTORC1.

Zhang Zhihong (Shanxi Medical University.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, China
Zhang Zhihong (Shanxi Medical University.role: Senior author of a study showing that the lncRNA LINP1 protects irradiated skin cells from radiation-induced senescence through the mTOR–p53 axis
Zhang Zhihong (Shanxi Medical University.sub: Corresponding author · Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health · Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, China
story: Zhang Zhihong is the corresponding author (with a personal institutional email on record) of the 2026 Mol Cell Biochem paper identifying the lncRNA LINP1 as a radioprotective factor in skin — it binds the FAT domain of mTOR and blocks its interaction with p53, holding off radiation-induced senescence in keratinocytes, validated in human skin explants.

Affiliated with the MOE Key Laboratory of Coal Environmental Pathogenicity and Prevention and the Center for Ecological Public Health Security of Yellow River Basin — consistent with a senior environmental-health/toxicology PI. Note: shares an identical name with a different co-author at Beihua University (see separate entry) — the two are distinct people confirmed by different institutions, fields, and non-overlapping co-author lists.

highlights.LIANG2026: Corresponding author on the study showing LINP1 suppresses radiation-induced keratinocyte senescence by blocking the mTOR–p53 interaction.

Zhang Zhihong (Beihua University).lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, College of Pharmacy, Beihua University, Jilin, China
Zhang Zhihong (Beihua University).role: Pharmacology researcher who contributed to a study showing that forsythoside A eases hypertensive kidney damage by promoting mitophagy and blocking ferroptosis via the ASCL1–CCNB1/mTOR pathway
Zhang Zhihong (Beihua University).sub: Pharmacology researcher · College of Pharmacy · Beihua University, Jilin, China
story: Zhang Zhihong is part of a recurring pharmacology research group at Beihua University's College of Pharmacy. In this 2026 J Ethnopharmacol study, the group showed that Forsythoside A — a compound from Forsythia suspensa — protects the kidney in hypertension models by promoting mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria) and blocking ferroptosis (iron-dependent cell death) through the ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR pathway.

The same group, with overlapping co-authors, published a related 2025 paper on Schisanhenol inhibiting hepatocellular carcinoma cell proliferation with the identical affiliation for this Zhang Zhihong, confirming a recurring, locatable member of this specific lab — distinct from the Shanxi Medical University researcher of the same name, with no institutional or co-author overlap between the two.

highlights.CUI2026: Co-author on the study showing Forsythoside A promotes mitophagy and inhibits ferroptosis via the ASCL1-CCNB1/mTOR pathway in hypertensive nephropathy.

Korolchuk VI.lab_name: Korolchuk Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University
Korolchuk VI.role: Showed that where lysosomes sit inside the cell tunes mTORC1 activity to nutrient supply. His Newcastle lab found that senescent cells can no longer switch mTORC1 off when nutrients or growth factors are withdrawn, and studies how autophagy and mitophagy decline with age
Korolchuk VI.sub: Professor of Cell Biology, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (since 2024) · Reader, Newcastle University (2017–2024) · Lecturer, Institute of Ageing and Health, Newcastle University (2011–2017) · postdoc, University of Cambridge (2003–2011, David Rubinsztein lab) · postdoc, University of Bristol (2000–2003) · PhD in Biochemistry, Institute of Biochemistry, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Kyiv (2000)
story: In 2011, working in David Rubinsztein's lab in Cambridge, Korolchuk showed that mTORC1 activity depends on something nobody had been treating as a variable: where the lysosome physically sits in the cell. With nutrients available, lysosomes move out towards the cell periphery, close to the plasma-membrane signalling modules, and mTORC1 is active there. Starvation changes intracellular pH and pulls them into a cluster around the nucleus, mTORC1 output falls, and autophagy is released. The same positioning also sets how fast autophagosomes fuse with lysosomes — so one variable governs both the start and the finish of autophagic flux.

Since starting his own group at Newcastle in 2011, he has worked the other end of the same problem: what mTORC1 does in cells that have stopped dividing. His lab showed that in senescent human cells mTORC1 is constitutively active and deaf to the removal of serum or amino acids, and that the fault lies upstream — a depolarised plasma membrane, defective primary cilia, and an internal amino acid pool kept topped up by autophagy. Correct those inputs and the cells die, which makes persistent mTORC1 signalling a survival dependency of senescent cells rather than a side effect of senescence.

More recently the lab has tied rapamycin's effect on cellular ageing to mitochondrial housekeeping: healthy primary human cells run a high level of basal mitophagy that shuts down in senescence, and reactivating it turned out to be necessary for the anti-senescence effect of both rapamycin and NAD precursors. Alongside the research, Korolchuk is the human selector behind Autophagy and mTOR (bims-auttor), the weekly curated literature report on biomed.news that has been running since February 2019 — the same slice of the literature this Atlas curates.

highlights.KOR2011: First author: showed lysosomal positioning coordinates mTORC1 signalling with autophagic flux, adding a spatial axis to nutrient sensing.
highlights.CAR2017: Senior author: explained why mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent cells, and that they depend on it to survive.
highlights.KEL2024: Senior author: reactivation of basal mitophagy is required for the anti-senescence effect of rapamycin and NAD precursors.
highlights.COR2018: Co-author: in nfkb1 mice rapamycin improved healthspan and lowered senescence markers without extending lifespan or reducing inflammaging.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author on the Cell study showing G3BP1/2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and thereby suppress mTORC1.

Kamada Y.lab_name: National Institute for Basic Biology, Okazaki
Kamada Y.role: Showed as first author that TOR keeps autophagy switched off in yeast by controlling the Atg1 (Apg1) kinase complex, and has studied TOR's control of autophagy ever since
Kamada Y.sub: Assistant Professor, National Institute for Basic Biology, National Institutes of Natural Sciences, Okazaki, Japan · ORCID 0000-0001-7395-660X
story: In 2000, in Yoshinori Ohsumi's group, Kamada asked a question that sounds simple and was not: how does TOR actually stop a cell from digesting itself? The answer turned out to be a phosphorylation switch one step upstream of the autophagy machinery. Starving the cells, or treating them with rapamycin, raised the kinase activity of Apg1 (now Atg1, the yeast counterpart of mammalian ULK1). TOR was keeping Apg13 hyperphosphorylated, and phosphorylated Apg13 binds Apg1 poorly. Remove TOR signalling and Apg13 loses its phosphates, binds Apg1, and autophagy starts.

The same paper drew a line that is easy to miss: the Apg1–Apg13 association is needed for autophagy but not for the Cvt pathway, a related vesicle route that uses many of the same proteins during normal growth. That made the Apg1 complex a switch between two transport systems rather than a simple on/off for one, which is why the finding survived the move from yeast to mammals.

His group at NIBB still works on TORC1 in budding yeast, and the NIBB page lists the same three threads: how amino acids regulate TORC1, how TORC1 controls autophagy through Atg13 phosphorylation, and how TORC1 acts on eIF4E-binding proteins. The mammalian version of his 2000 result (ULK1–ATG13–FIP200) was published nine years later.

highlights.KAM2000: First author: TOR represses autophagy by keeping Apg13 hyperphosphorylated, so it cannot bind and activate the Apg1 kinase.
