Zalzala S.role: Family physician who co-founded AgelessRx and led PEARL, a year-long randomised trial of low-dose intermittent rapamycin in healthy older adults
Zalzala S.sub: Founder and Medical Director, Root Causes Medical · Co-Founder and Chief Medical Officer, AgelessRx · Family physician, Dearborn, Michigan · Residency in Family Medicine, Wayne State University (2009–2012) · MD, Wayne State University School of Medicine (2009) · Board certified in Family Medicine, American Board of Family Medicine
story: Zalzala is the senior author of MOE2025 and one of the four people the paper credits with designing and implementing the study. PEARL (NCT04488601) was a 48-week, decentralized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial sponsored by AgelessRx with the University of California, Los Angeles as collaborator, comparing 5 mg or 10 mg of compounded rapamycin per week against placebo in healthy adults aged 50 to 85. It is the first completed long-term randomized trial of rapamycin taken for ageing itself rather than for a disease.

The pre-registered primary endpoint - visceral fat measured by DXA - did not move at all (p = 0.942). Because the endpoint had been fixed in advance, the trial has to report a null result, and the more interesting secondary findings, such as better lean tissue mass and less self-reported pain in women on the 10 mg dose, stay where they belong: as hypotheses for the next trial rather than as conclusions. Adverse events were comparable across all three arms, which is the safety answer the study was mainly built to give.

He is a board-certified family physician who trained at Wayne State University in Detroit and practised in Dearborn, Michigan, before co-founding AgelessRx, a telemedicine company that prescribes off-label longevity drugs, and serving as its chief medical officer; he also founded the clinic Root Causes Medical. The paper states the obvious conflict openly: all seven authors are employees and shareholders of AgelessRx, which is why the pre-registered, placebo-controlled design and the honest reporting of the null primary endpoint matter so much here.

highlights.MOE2025: Senior author; the paper's author contributions list him among the four people who designed and implemented the PEARL trial.

Moel M.role: Analyses trial and real-world data on repurposed longevity drugs at AgelessRx and led the reporting of the PEARL rapamycin trial
Moel M.sub: Co-Founder, AgelessRx · Researcher, Division of Research and Applied Sciences, AgelessRx · Research in computational microbial ecology, Department of Biology, Boston University · BA in Neurobiology, Boston University
story: Moel is the first author of MOE2025, the PEARL trial report, and one of the three people the paper credits with the data analysis. That analysis is what makes the paper worth reading: the pre-registered primary endpoint, visceral fat on a DXA scan, moved essentially not at all (p = 0.942), and the report says so plainly instead of promoting a secondary finding into the headline.

The secondary results he analysed are narrower than the press coverage suggested. Among women taking 10 mg of rapamycin weekly, lean tissue mass and self-reported pain improved; participants on 5 mg reported better emotional well-being and general health; blood biomarkers stayed inside normal ranges and adverse events were similar in all three groups. With 114 people finishing 48 weeks, these are signals worth chasing in a properly powered follow-up, not evidence that the drug works.

Before he moved into longevity medicine he was at Boston University, where he took a BA in neurobiology and co-authored a computational study with Daniel Segre's group on 'costless' metabolites - compounds a bacterium can release without paying any growth penalty, which helps explain how stable cross-feeding between species can arise at all. At AgelessRx he has stayed on the data side, also co-authoring the company's work on how much rapamycin actually reaches the blood from compounded versus commercial formulations.

highlights.MOE2025: First author; the paper's author contributions list him as one of the three people who performed the data analysis for the PEARL trial.

Harinath G.lab_name: Division of Research and Applied Sciences, AgelessRx (Ann Arbor, MI)
Harinath G.role: Designs, analyses and writes up human studies of repurposed drugs such as rapamycin at a longevity telehealth company, turning trial and real-world prescription data into peer-reviewed evidence
Harinath G.sub: Research Scientist, Division of Research and Applied Sciences, AgelessRx, Ann Arbor, MI · Researcher, Driscoll Lab, Department of Molecular Biology & Biochemistry, Rutgers University · Contributor, NIA Caenorhabditis Intervention Testing Program (CITP)
story: Harinath is the second author of the PEARL trial report, the first completed year-long randomized, placebo-controlled trial of rapamycin taken for healthy human aging rather than for disease (NCT04488601, AgelessRx as sponsor with UCLA as collaborator). Participants aged 50–85 took either placebo or 5 mg or 10 mg of compounded rapamycin once a week for 48 weeks, and the endpoint the team had committed to in advance was visceral fat measured by DXA scan. That endpoint did not move at all, while secondary measures — lean tissue mass and self-reported pain in women on 10 mg, and self-reported well-being on 5 mg — did improve.

His own first-author work explains part of why a null result there is hard to interpret. In a 2025 GeroScience paper he showed that compounded rapamycin, the formulation PEARL used, reaches only about 31% of the blood level per milligram that commercial sirolimus does, that blood levels peak roughly two days after a dose, and that different people on the same dose end up in very different places. In practical terms: a weekly 10 mg compounded tablet may inhibit mTOR far less than the number on the label suggests, which is an argument for measuring rapamycin in blood rather than trusting the dose.

Before joining AgelessRx he worked in Monica Driscoll's lab at Rutgers on the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, co-authoring studies on how swim exercise protects aging muscle and neurons, how spaceflight changes neuronal shape, and how metformin and antioxidants extend or shorten life depending on the animal's genetic background. That last theme carries into his human work: in a 2024 review he argued that quality-of-life questionnaires such as the SF-36 should count as real endpoints in geroscience trials, because waiting decades for disease and death outcomes is not a practical way to test drugs meant to keep people healthy.

highlights.MOE2025: Second author on the PEARL results paper, the AgelessRx report of the 48-week safety profile, DXA body-composition outcomes and quality-of-life measures for weekly low-dose rapamycin.

Ali ES.lab_name: Ali Lab (Metabolism & Signaling), Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, University of Kentucky College of Medicine
Ali ES.role: Showed as a Ben-Sahra-lab postdoc that ERK2 directly activates the purine-synthesis enzyme PFAS, and that mTORC1 increases bicarbonate import through SLC4A7 to fuel nucleotide synthesis. His Kentucky lab studies how growth signals control nucleotide metabolism in cancer
Ali ES.sub: Assistant Professor of Cancer Metabolism, Department of Toxicology and Cancer Biology, University of Kentucky College of Medicine (since 2024); Markey Cancer Center and Center for Cancer and Metabolism · postdoc, Issam Ben-Sahra lab, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (2017–2024) · PhD, Flinders University, Adelaide (Greg Barritt lab) · MS, Stockholm University (Göran Widmalm lab)
story: A dividing cell needs nucleotides, and nucleotides need carbon. Ali showed in ALI2022 that mTORC1 does not only switch on the enzymes that build them – it also organises the delivery of the raw material. Through S6K and the translation factor eIF4B, mTORC1 selectively raises translation of the mRNA for SLC4A7, a sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter, so the cell pulls in more bicarbonate from its surroundings. Take SLC4A7 away from cells with hyperactive mTORC1 and flux through both purine and pyrimidine synthesis drops, along with cell and tumour growth – and the internal pH does not budge, so the transporter is acting as a supply line, not as a pH valve.

Two years earlier he had drawn a boundary around the same claim. In ALI2020 he found that the other big growth pathway reaches purine synthesis by its own route: ERK2, but not its close relative ERK1, phosphorylates the enzyme PFAS at threonine 619. Because this is a direct modification of the enzyme rather than a change in how much of it is made, the effect lands within minutes. A cell with a PFAS that cannot be phosphorylated makes fewer purines, forms fewer colonies and grows smaller tumours – so in a RAS-driven tumour, purine supply cannot be read from mTORC1 activity alone.

He trained as a carbohydrate chemist in Stockholm and then as a liver physiologist at Flinders, where he worked on how fat accumulation deranges calcium handling in hepatocytes, before joining Issam Ben-Sahra at Northwestern. There he also contributed to VIL2021, which turned the SAM story around: the Atlas already had SAMTOR as a sensor of S-adenosylmethionine, and that paper showed mTORC1 also controls how much SAM the cell makes. Since 2024 he has run his own laboratory at the University of Kentucky, asking how tumours keep their nucleotide supply running and where that supply can be cut.

highlights.ALI2022: First author; showed mTORC1 drives SLC4A7 translation to import bicarbonate and keep de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis running.
highlights.ALI2020: First author; found that ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS at T619, a fast, posttranslational route to purine synthesis that runs parallel to mTORC1.
highlights.VIL2021: Co-author on the study showing mTORC1 raises SAM production and WTAP levels to tune m6A mRNA modification and protein synthesis.

Sahu U.lab_name: Department of Biochemical Engineering and Biotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi
Sahu U.role: Showed that the building blocks of RNA also tell mitochondria how fast to burn fuel
Sahu U.sub: Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemical Engineering and Biotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi (since 2026) · Research Assistant Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (2024–2026) · postdoc, Issam Ben-Sahra lab, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center (2017–2024) · PhD, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru (Pundi N. Rangarajan lab)
story: Nucleotides are usually described as the letters of DNA and RNA, and little else. Sahu's own headline finding is that one of them moonlights as a fuel-gauge signal. Working at Northwestern, he showed that UTP – a pyrimidine nucleotide – is the preferred partner of the enzyme TPK1, which manufactures thiamine pyrophosphate, the active form of vitamin B1. Mitochondria need that cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. So when a cell runs short of pyrimidines, TPK1 slows, the cofactor thins out, pyruvate oxidation drops, and the cell stops making new fat. A shortage of RNA letters becomes, several steps later, a shortage of lipid.

That result grew out of several years spent mapping how growth signalling arranges nucleotide supply in Issam Ben-Sahra's lab. In ALI2020 he worked on the discovery that ERK2 acts directly on the purine-synthesis enzyme PFAS – a fast chemical modification of the enzyme rather than a slow change in how much of it the cell makes. In VIL2021 he helped trace a different thread: mTORC1 pushes up production of SAM, the cell's universal methyl donor, and through it the m6A marks placed on mRNA, which in turn set the pace of protein synthesis.

He came to this from an unlikely direction. His PhD at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru was on the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris, where he characterised the zinc-finger transcription factor Mxr1p as a master switch for how the yeast handles methanol, acetate and amino acids as carbon sources. Since June 2026 he has run his own group at IIT Delhi, using metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics and CRISPR screens to ask how these regulatory circuits go wrong in metabolic disease.

highlights.ALI2020: Second author; contributed to the finding that ERK2 phosphorylates the purine-synthesis enzyme PFAS, a fast posttranslational route to nucleotide supply running parallel to mTORC1.
highlights.VIL2021: Second author; helped show that mTORC1 raises SAM synthesis and m6A mRNA modification to control the rate of protein synthesis.

O'Hara BP.role: As lab manager of Issam Ben-Sahra's lab at Northwestern, contributed to its studies of how mTORC1 and ERK control nucleotide synthesis, SAM production and bicarbonate import
O'Hara BP.sub: Associate Director, Lab Manager, Dispatch Bio (since 2022) · Research Lab Manager, Issam Ben-Sahra lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Genetics, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (2019–2022) · research and postdoctoral-affairs roles, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis (2006–2019), including the Department of Genetics · MSc, Biochemistry, University of Bath
story: Behind almost every fast-moving metabolism lab there is someone who keeps the cell lines alive, the reagents stocked and the experiments reproducible – and who is often at the bench doing the work as well. For three years that person in Issam Ben-Sahra's lab at Northwestern was Brendan O'Hara, and his name sits on the run of papers that mapped how growth signalling arranges the supply of nucleotides: the ERK2–PFAS link (ALI2020), the SAM and m6A route from mTORC1 to protein synthesis (VIL2021), and the mTORC1–SLC4A7 bicarbonate import axis (ALI2022).

He arrived there from St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis, where he spent more than a decade in research and postdoctoral-affairs roles. In the Department of Genetics he was a co-author on the 2018 report proposing mTORC3 – a third, rapamycin-insensitive mTOR assembly built around the transcription factor ETV7, offered as one explanation for why rapamycin so often disappoints as a cancer drug. That claim remains debated, but it is a reminder that the standard two-complex picture of mTOR has been challenged from inside the field.

Since 2022 he has worked in industry, as lab manager at the cancer-immunotherapy start-up Dispatch Bio, while continuing to appear as a co-author on work begun at Northwestern – including the 2024 study showing that matrix stiffness pushes cells to accumulate sorbitol, which then helps proteins condense into droplets.

highlights.ALI2022: Co-author; contributed to the work showing mTORC1 raises SLC4A7 translation to import bicarbonate for de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis.
highlights.ALI2020: Co-author on the discovery that ERK2 phosphorylates PFAS at T619, speeding up purine synthesis without changing how much enzyme is present.
highlights.VIL2021: Co-author on the study linking mTORC1 to SAM synthesis, m6A mRNA modification and the control of protein synthesis.

Hong S.role: First-authored the cryo-EM structure identifying TM6SF1 as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1
Hong S.sub: Hobbs Lab & Li (Xiaochun) Lab, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center
story: Sen Hong is a structural biologist working across the Hobbs and Li labs at UT Southwestern, applying cryo-electron microscopy to membrane proteins involved in lipid and cholesterol biology.

highlights.HON2026: First-authored the cryo-EM structure of TM6SF1, showing the protein binds cholesterol and directly engages LAMTOR1 to regulate mTORC1 signaling.

Li X.role: Solves cryo-EM structures of cholesterol-sensing membrane proteins, including the new mTORC1 regulator TM6SF1
Li X.sub: Eugene McDermott Distinguished Chair in Molecular Genetics, UT Southwestern · PhD, Tsinghua University · postdoc with Günter Blobel, Rockefeller University
story: Xiaochun Li earned his PhD in structural biology at Tsinghua University in 2012, then trained as a postdoctoral fellow with Nobel laureate Günter Blobel at Rockefeller University. In 2017 he joined the Department of Molecular Genetics at UT Southwestern, working alongside Nobel laureates Joseph Goldstein and Michael Brown.

His lab uses cryo-electron microscopy and protein engineering to study membrane proteins with Sterol-Sensing Domains — including Niemann-Pick C1, HMG-CoA reductase, and the Hedgehog receptors Patched and Dispatched — that govern how cells sense and traffic cholesterol.
He holds the Eugene McDermott Distinguished Chair in Molecular Genetics and has received the Damon Runyon–Rachleff Innovation Award and the American Heart Association Established Investigator Award.

highlights.HON2026: Senior-authored the cryo-EM structure of TM6SF1, identifying it as a lysosomal cholesterol-binding regulator of mTORC1 signaling via LAMTOR1.

Halle JL.lab_name: Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory, University of Tennessee Health Science Center
Halle JL.role: Muscle-biology researcher studying how cancer, chemotherapy and cachexia disrupt skeletal-muscle protein turnover and autophagy
Halle JL.sub: Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory, Division of Regenerative and Rehabilitation Sciences, University of Tennessee Health Science Center · Aging and Metabolism Research Program, Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation
story: Halle works in James Carson's Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory, where her research centers on how cancer and its treatment disrupt skeletal muscle, including the feeding regulation of muscle protein synthesis in tumour-bearing mice and the mechanisms by which chemotherapy damages muscle independent of the tumour itself.

In the 2026 myotube study, she led the experiments dissecting how FOLFOX chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin and oxaliplatin) disrupts autophagy flux and protein synthesis in cultured muscle cells through altered mTORC1 and AMPK signalling, and tested whether the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin or the AMPK activator metformin could reverse the damage.

highlights.HAL2026: First author; led the myotube experiments testing how FOLFOX chemotherapy disrupts mTORC1/AMPK-regulated autophagy flux and protein synthesis, and whether rapamycin could restore it.

Carson JA.lab_name: Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory, University of Tennessee Health Science Center
Carson JA.role: Muscle physiologist studying cancer-associated cachexia and how chemotherapy and exercise remodel skeletal-muscle metabolism
Carson JA.sub: Senior Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Studies, College of Health Professions, University of Tennessee Health Science Center (since 2018) · Director and Chief, Regenerative and Rehabilitation Sciences Division, Tennessee Institute for Regenerative Medicine · 19 years on faculty at the University of South Carolina, where he built its muscle-biology research program and directed its Exercise Science PhD program
story: Carson leads the Integrative Muscle Biology Laboratory and is among the field's established voices on cancer-associated cachexia — the muscle wasting that accompanies tumours and their treatment. Before moving to the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in 2018, he spent 19 years at the University of South Carolina building a muscle-biology research program and growing its Exercise Science doctoral program into a nationally top-ranked one.

His laboratory combines in vivo and in vitro models to examine how mechanical, inflammatory and hormonal signals converge on skeletal-muscle anabolic and metabolic plasticity. The 2026 study he senior-authored asked a narrower version of that question: whether the muscle damage caused by FOLFOX chemotherapy runs through mTORC1 and AMPK's control of autophagy, and whether rapamycin — by restoring autophagy flux — could partly undo it.

highlights.HAL2026: Senior and corresponding author; his laboratory's long-standing work on cancer-associated cachexia framed the study's focus on chemotherapy-induced disruption of muscle mTORC1/AMPK signalling.

Yang Y.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing
Yang Y.role: Showed as first author that the liver-secreted protein hepassocin protects against age-related liver senescence and helps the liver regenerate
Yang Y.sub: State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing · Department of Engineering Physics, Tsinghua University, Beijing
story: Yang is based at the State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics in Beijing, where the 2026 study he led asked why aged livers regenerate so poorly after injury. The team traced the answer to Hepassocin (HPS), a liver-secreted hormone whose levels fall with age in both mice and elderly humans, and that normally activates AMPK — restraining mTOR — through a relay running from a surface receptor complex to the LKB1 kinase.

In mice engineered to lack HPS, that restraint failed: aged animals showed elevated mTOR activity, impaired autophagy, worsened cellular senescence, and a severely blunted capacity to regrow liver tissue after partial hepatectomy. Restoring AMPK signalling, either with the drug AICAR or with HPS itself, rescued the aging phenotype, pointing to the HPS-AMPK-mTOR axis as a lever for age-related liver decline.

highlights.YAN2026B: First author; led the identification of Hepassocin (HPS) as an AMPK-activating hepatokine that restrains mTOR and protects against age-related liver senescence and regeneration failure.

Yang X.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing
Yang X.role: Showed as senior author that the liver-secreted protein hepassocin protects against age-related liver senescence and helps the liver regenerate
Yang X.sub: Corresponding author, State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, National Center for Protein Sciences (Beijing), Academy of Military Medical Sciences · School of Pharmacy, Guangdong Pharmaceutical University · School of Basic Medical Sciences, University of South China
story: Yang is the corresponding author on the 2026 study identifying Hepassocin (HPS) as a hepatokine that keeps aging livers regenerating. His laboratory traced how HPS activates AMPK through an ANXA2-ERK-p90RSK-LKB1 relay, restraining mTOR activity, and showed that this axis weakens with age — leaving HPS-deficient aged mice with elevated mTOR signalling, impaired autophagy, and a much-reduced ability to recover liver mass after injury.
The work points to restoring HPS or AMPK signalling, rather than blocking mTOR directly, as a route to counteracting age-related liver dysfunction and regeneration failure.

highlights.YAN2026B: Senior and corresponding author; his laboratory's proteomics platform identified Hepassocin as a novel AMPK-activating hepatokine that protects against liver senescence and regeneration failure.

Sun L.lab_name: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University)
Sun L.role: Researcher studying phosphorylation-based control of autophagy initiation and its role in metabolic liver disease
Sun L.sub: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University), Chongqing, China
story: Sun is based in the Department of Clinical Biochemistry at Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) in Chongqing, China. In the 2026 Nature Communications study, he led the work uncovering how the deubiquitinase OTUB1 is switched on by starvation: ERK phosphorylates OTUB1, stabilizing it against degradation and letting it drive up DEPTOR, a natural brake on mTOR.

The team showed in mice that restoring this fasting-triggered ERK-OTUB1-DEPTOR-mTOR relay could counteract the mTOR-activating effect of a Western diet and ease progression of MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease), offering a mechanistic account of why fasting benefits the liver.

highlights.SUN2026B: First author; led the identification of the ERK-OTUB1-DEPTOR axis that inhibits mTOR and drives starvation-induced autophagy, with relevance to fasting's protective effect against MASLD.

Lian J.lab_name: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University)
Lian J.role: Biochemist studying deubiquitinase signalling in autophagy and metabolic disease
Lian J.sub: Corresponding author, Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University), Chongqing, China
story: Lian is a corresponding author in the Department of Clinical Biochemistry at Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) in Chongqing, China. The 2026 study from his group traced how cells sense starvation at the molecular level: ERK-driven phosphorylation stabilizes the deubiquitinase OTUB1, which in turn boosts DEPTOR to hold mTOR in check and switch on autophagy.

The work extended this mechanism to disease relevance, showing in a mouse model that reactivating the fasting-triggered OTUB1-mTOR axis could blunt Western-diet-driven mTOR activation and slow the progression of MASLD.

highlights.SUN2026B: Corresponding author; his laboratory identified the phosphorylation-dependent OTUB1-DEPTOR-mTOR mechanism linking starvation to autophagy initiation and its relevance to fasting-based protection against MASLD.

Kondratov RV.lab_name: Kondratov Lab, Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease, Cleveland State University
Kondratov RV.role: Showed the circadian clock protein BMAL1 gates TOR/mTOR signaling to control aging, and that calorie restriction's lifespan benefits require a working circadian clock
Kondratov RV.sub: Professor & Associate VP for Research, Cleveland State University · Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease
story: Roman Kondratov leads a laboratory at Cleveland State University studying how the circadian clock — the internal 24-hour timekeeping system — shapes metabolism, cardiovascular physiology, and aging. His lab reported that mice lacking BMAL1, the core circadian clock protein, develop an early-aging syndrome: a lifespan of about 9 months versus 28 months in normal mice, along with sarcopenia, osteoporosis, cataracts, and other age-related pathologies.

Because BMAL1 is a transcription factor that can influence many pathways, the lab has worked out which downstream systems carry the aging signal, including TOR signaling, the Sirtuin pathway, and IGF/IGFR signaling — pathways that govern cell growth and the organism's response to nutrients and stress. A parallel line of work in the lab established that calorie restriction, one of the most robust lifespan-extending interventions known, works partly by resetting circadian rhythms in gene expression, and that an intact circadian clock is necessary for calorie restriction to extend lifespan.

That combination of circadian timing and mTOR signaling is the throughline of the lab's more recent work, including showing that calorie restriction's effect on liver mTOR signaling is time-of-day dependent — the same theme carried into VEL2026, comparing calorie restriction to fasting-refeeding cycles.

highlights.VEL2026: Senior/corresponding author; showed caloric restriction engages anticipatory, circadian-clock-aligned control of hepatic mTOR signaling, distinct from the reactive, cue-driven signaling seen under fasting-refeeding cycles.

Velingkaar N.lab_name: Kondratov Lab, Cleveland State University (where this work was done)
Velingkaar N.role: Postdoctoral fellow studying how the circadian clock times caloric restriction's effects on liver mTOR signaling and metabolism
Velingkaar N.sub: Postdoctoral Fellow, Kondratov Lab, Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Disease, Cleveland State University
story: Nikkhil Velingkaar trained as a PhD student in the Kondratov lab at Cleveland State University, where his dissertation research (supported by a CSU Dissertation Research Award) examined how internal circadian clocks interact to regulate daily rhythms in metabolic activity. He has continued in the lab as a postdoctoral fellow.

His work has focused on calorie restriction as a circadian phenomenon: earlier first-author studies from the lab showed that calorie restriction's effect on liver mTOR signaling depends on time of day, and that a two-meal calorie-restriction schedule induces 12-hour metabolic rhythms and improves glucose homeostasis. VEL2026 extends that line of work by directly comparing calorie restriction to fasting-refeeding cycles matched for food intake and fasting duration.

highlights.VEL2026: First author; distinguished caloric restriction's anticipatory, clock-aligned metabolic control (including hepatic mTOR signaling) from the reactive signaling seen under fasting-refeeding cycles.

Singh M.lab_name: Mayo Clinic, Department of Cardiovascular Diseases
Singh M.role: Interventional cardiologist and professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic; corresponding author on a 2026 trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
Singh M.sub: Mayo Clinic College of Medicine and Science · Rochester, MN
story: Mandeep Singh is a professor of medicine and interventional cardiologist in the Department of Cardiovascular Diseases at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, where he trained as an interventional cardiology fellow in the late 1990s.

In 2026 he was the corresponding author on a trial testing rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), working alongside Mayo's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging and University of Wisconsin-Madison mTOR/aging researchers James Kirkland and Dudley Lamming.

highlights.LAN2026: Corresponding author on a trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older HFpEF patients.

Marchetti L.lab_name: Laboratory of Computational Modeling, CIBIO, University of Trento / COSBI
Marchetti L.role: Computational biologist building quantitative systems-pharmacology and disease models; senior author on a 2026 survival analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial
Marchetti L.sub: University of Trento (CIBIO) · Fondazione COSBI, Rovereto
story: Luca Marchetti holds a PhD in computer science from the University of Verona and is an associate professor in the CIBIO department at the University of Trento, where he heads the Laboratory of Computational Modeling. He is also a consultant at the Microsoft Research - University of Trento Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI).

His work applies quantitative systems pharmacology and physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modeling, often with machine learning, to complex disease data. In 2026 he was senior author on a multivariate survival analysis of the RAP-ALS clinical trial of rapamycin in ALS patients, which found a signal of longer survival in treated C9orf72 mutation carriers.

highlights.DEN2026B: Senior author on the RAP-ALS multivariate survival analysis, which found a survival signal in rapamycin-treated C9orf72 carriers.

Rainero E.lab_name: Rainero Lab, School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield
Rainero E.role: Studies how cancer cells use the extracellular matrix as a nutrient and signaling source; senior author on a 2026 study linking collagen I to mTORC1 activation in cancer cells
Rainero E.sub: University of Sheffield, School of Biosciences
story: Elena Rainero leads a lab in the School of Biosciences at the University of Sheffield studying the crosstalk between the extracellular matrix (ECM), integrin trafficking and cancer cell metabolism, including how cancer cells internalise and repurpose ECM components as a nutrient source under metabolic stress.

In 2026 her lab reported that collagen I drives alpha2beta1 integrin-dependent mTORC1/S6 activation and boosts amino acid import via the LAT1-4F2hc transporter, letting breast and pancreatic cancer cells survive and grow in nutrient-poor, collagen-rich tumor stroma.

highlights.NAZ2026: Senior author showing collagen I drives mTORC1/S6 activation and LAT1-4F2hc-mediated amino acid import in cancer cells.

Raffel S.role: Studies metabolic vulnerabilities of leukemia stem cells; senior author on a 2026 Blood paper on IDH3, citrate and mTORC1 in AML stem cell drug resistance
Raffel S.sub: Heidelberg University Hospital · Emmy Noether Group (DFG)
story: Simon Raffel runs an independent Emmy Noether research group at Heidelberg University Hospital studying the metabolic biology of leukemia stem cells (LSCs), building on earlier work (recognised with the 2018 Walter Schulz Prize) on amino acid breakdown in leukemia stem cells. He remains affiliated with HI-STEM and the Heidelberg-based LeukoSyStem consortium.

In 2026 his lab identified the TCA-cycle enzyme IDH3 as a selective regulator of AML leukemic stem cell maintenance: knocking down IDH3A raises intracellular citrate, activates AMPK and suppresses mTORC1, and sensitises resistant AML cells to the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax.

highlights.DEM2026: Senior author identifying the IDH3A-citrate-AMPK-mTORC1 axis as a route to overcome venetoclax resistance in AML stem cells.

Zhou X.role: Built TORCAR, the first genetically encoded reporter that lets mTORC1 activity be watched in living cells
Zhou X.sub: Senior Scientist, Eikon Therapeutics · formerly postdoc (Johns Hopkins, 2010–2015) and Associate Project Scientist (UC San Diego, 2015–2022) in Jin Zhang's lab · PhD, Medicinal Chemistry, University of Minnesota
story: Xin Zhou earned a PhD in medicinal chemistry at the University of Minnesota, then joined Jin Zhang's lab at Johns Hopkins as a postdoc in 2010. The lab builds fluorescent sensors that show when an enzyme is working inside a living cell. When the lab moved to UC San Diego in 2015, Zhou moved with it as an associate project scientist and stayed until 2022, then went to industry as a scientist at Eikon Therapeutics in California.

TORCAR is a small protein that mTORC1 phosphorylates, built so that the phosphorylation changes how two fluorescent parts pass energy to each other (FRET). A microscope can read that change in a single living cell, second by second. Before this, mTORC1 activity was measured by grinding up many cells at fixed time points. With TORCAR the team saw mTORC1 working not only at the lysosome but also in the cytosol, the nucleus and at the plasma membrane, and saw a short calcium spike after growth-factor stimulation feed into mTORC1 activity.

highlights.ZHO2015: First author on TORCAR, a FRET sensor that shows mTORC1 activity changing in living cells and in different parts of the cell, depending on which signal switched it on.

Kubota H.lab_name: Division of Integrated Omics, Kyushu University
Kubota H.role: Systems biologist who showed that the insulin pathway carries different messages in the timing of its signal, and that S6K, the mTORC1 target, reads only the fast part
Kubota H.sub: Professor, Division of Integrated Omics, Research Center for Transomics Medicine, Medical Institute of Bioregulation, Kyushu University · PhD in Science, University of Tokyo
story: Hiroyuki Kubota earned his doctorate at the University of Tokyo in 2001 and spent the following years there, from 2009 as an assistant professor in Shinya Kuroda's systems biology group. In 2014 he became a professor at Kyushu University's Medical Institute of Bioregulation, where his lab combines measurements of many molecular layers at once (proteins, their phosphorylation, metabolites) with mathematical models.

His two studies in the Atlas ask one question at two scales: can a cell tell a short burst of insulin from a steady level? In rat liver cells (KUB2012) and then in living rats (KUB2018), the answer was yes. The same pathway passes on both patterns, and each downstream molecule picks the part it responds to. S6K, which sits directly under mTORC1, followed the quick pulse. G6Pase, a glucose-making enzyme, followed the steady baseline. That makes the timing of a signal, not only its size, part of the message.

highlights.KUB2012: First author. In liver cells, a short insulin pulse and a steady insulin dose were passed through AKT as two different time patterns, and S6K responded only to the fast one.
highlights.KUB2018: First author. The in-vivo follow-up in rat liver: the insulin receptor carries every insulin pattern, and downstream molecules pick out different parts of it, with S6K reading the pulse-like extra secretion.

Kubota H.credit: Portrait: Medical Institute of Bioregulation, Kyushu University

Kuroda S.lab_name: Kuroda Lab (Systems Biology), University of Tokyo
Kuroda S.role: Leads a systems biology lab that studies how cells decode the timing of hormone signals, with insulin and mTORC1-S6K as the main test case
Kuroda S.sub: Professor, Department of Biological Sciences, Graduate School of Science, The University of Tokyo
story: Shinya Kuroda runs the systems biology laboratory in the University of Tokyo's Department of Biological Sciences. His group starts from a simple observation: the same stimulus can lead to different outcomes depending on how it arrives over time. They pair experiments with computer models to work out how signalling networks turn a pattern into a decision, and more recently how whole metabolic networks shift in obesity.

He is senior author on both Atlas studies on this idea, KUB2012 in cultured liver cells and KUB2018 in the liver of living rats. Together they show that insulin information is split by timing. S6K, the kinase mTORC1 switches on, responds to fast insulin pulses, while other targets respond to the slow baseline. This is one of the clearest cases in the Atlas where the shape of a signal over time matters as much as how strong it is, which is the question behind Oliver's focus on mTOR dynamics.

highlights.KUB2012: Senior author. Showed that the AKT pathway carries pulse and sustained insulin signals as separate time patterns, which downstream targets such as S6K decode selectively.
highlights.KUB2018: Senior author. Confirmed the same timing code in living rat liver and used modelling to explain it through network structure, sensitivity and time constants.

Zhang J.lab_name: Jin Zhang Lab, UC San Diego
Zhang J.role: Builds fluorescent biosensors that show where and when signalling enzymes are active inside living cells; senior author of TORCAR, the first live-cell reporter of mTORC1
Zhang J.sub: Vice Chair and Professor of Pharmacology, UC San Diego School of Medicine (also Bioengineering and Chemistry & Biochemistry) · PhD, University of Chicago
story: Jin Zhang studied chemistry at Tsinghua University, earned her PhD at the University of Chicago and trained as a postdoc with Roger Tsien and Susan Taylor at UC San Diego. She led a lab at Johns Hopkins from 2003 and moved it back to UC San Diego in 2015. Her group makes genetically encoded sensors, proteins that glow differently when a particular kinase touches them, and uses them to map signalling inside single cells.

TORCAR, from her Johns Hopkins lab, applied that approach to mTORC1. It showed mTORC1 activity in several places at once (lysosome, cytosol, nucleus, plasma membrane) and showed that growth factors and amino acids light up different sets of those places. Watching mTORC1 in real time in one cell is the kind of measurement that later studies of mTORC1 oscillation depend on.

highlights.ZHO2015: Senior author on TORCAR, the first genetically encoded reporter of mTORC1 activity, which showed signal-specific mTORC1 activity in different parts of living cells.
